recommendations.text: Recommendations to the Irish authorities: - The Department of the Marine and Natural Resources, as the national competent authority should be given the legal powers to close down the production areas. - The supervision of the establishments should put more emphasis on documentary checks. In particular, attention should be given so that registration documents and ledger books are used according to their purpose. - Better formalisation of the classification procedures and of the design of monitoring programmes, specifically by making available written protocols, defined sampling points and procedures, would consolidate the system in place. - Shellfish should not be dispatched without being packed and labelled according to the Directive requirements, even when placed on the local market. - In the establishment concerned the microbiological analysis of final product should be organised so that the establishment will be provided with the results on a regular basis, ensuring a permanent control of the quality of the shellfish by the establishment itself. - Frequency of the inspections should be at such a level as to ensure full compliance of the establishments with the Directive.

Recommendations to the European Commission: - Further clarification is needed regarding the use, purpose and design of the registration document. - A working group should be established to update Directive 91/492/EEC. Microbiological and phytotoxicity aspects would have in particular to be considered, in order to better protect public health. The Irish authorities specifically asked the Commission to organise a working group. - DSP and biotoxin intercalibration test should be organised soon to ensure the same level of safety of the shellfish produced in the Member States. 6
The use of vaccine should not be considered at this time.

Consideration should be given to using the ELISA whey test especially on bulk milk samples that are positive to the milk ring test. This will have the effect of reducing the number of false positive MRT's.

Consideration should be given to using the Buffered rose bengal agglutination test (USDA card test) by the Veterinary inspector in herds which have demonstrated a reactor to other tests. This will have the effect of rapidly identifying additional within herd-infected animals and lead to their rapid removal thus avoiding subsequent spread. It can be carried out on the farm and it is efficient at identifying early infection.
Consideration should be given to increasing the range of the contiguous testing arrangements to two herds from the infected premises.
Consideration should be given to routine testing of the farm dog particularly in infected premises. If positive the dog should be isolated and therapeutically treated.

The Commission shall be informed as the recommendations are implemented and should be included in their presentation to the Commission for financial aid for the Brucella eradication programme for the year 2000. 12.2. To the Commission services: 12.2.1. The Commission services should organise an inspection mission to evaluate progress in two years time. 14

In the review of the provisions concerning knackers' yards, the Commission Services in charge of veterinary legislation should take into account the role of the knackeries in the fallen stock collection network.
Issues relating to record keeping, waste-water treatment, animal welfare, health protection of workers, should also be taken into account in the review. 11
The competent authority should consider prohibiting the use of the product used for the "decontamination" of MBM, until the product is approved as a feed-additive.4
The competent authority should consider measures to exclude foreign material from raw-material for feedingstuffs.
The Irish authorities should provide Commission Services regularly with data on the number of burial licences issued, justification for the licences and estimated number of un-licenced burial.
The competent authority should consider collecting and summarising the data in knackeries'intake records, as regards veterinary involvement and fallen stock.

The competent authority should include fallen stock in the national monitoring program of BSE. 4 The Irish Authorities are awaiting a decision by the EU Commission as to the precise status of products used to remove salmonella contamination. However, there has been an application of formaldehyde as a preservative of feedingstuffs in 1992 and the opinion of the Scientific Committee in Animal Nutrition is negative. The Commission has asked the Member states to prohibit the use of formaldehyde for salmonella decontamination in September -99 and October -99. 18 DG(SANCO)/1119/1999 MR Final
The non-compliances observed in the treatment of waste-water and sludge from knackeries should be corrected5.
The competent authority should prohibit the amputation of tails of dairy cattle.

The competent authority should consider giving detailed instructions on identity checks in slaughterhouses, marts and exit points and in particular, on corrective actions in cases where irregularities have been detected, in order to guarantee a uniform approach in this respect.
The competent authority should take actions to bring existing controls on bovine identification and registration in to line with Commission Regulation 2630/97/EC.
In order not to undermine the overall efficiency and credibility of the SRM controls, immediate action should be taken to correct non-critical deficiencies observed by the mission team.

The Irish authorities should enforce BSE monitoring activities in slaughterhouses, particularly as regards emergency slaughter and casualties and consider including casualties/emergencies in the monitoring program.

The competent authority should consider giving instructions on procedures to be followed as regards selection of animals to be sampled, clinical examination of suspect cases and ruling out of BSE to ensure a uniform approach and full compliance with Commission Decision 98/272/EC in particular amongst private practitioners.

The annual number of brains examined should be increased at least to the minimum requirement laid down in Commission Decision 98/272/EC. 5 Ireland understands that this is not part of the requirements for knackeries. The Irish Authorities have been reminded by means of a written note that this requirement is explicitly laid down in Article 3, 1st iondent of Commission Decision 95/348/EC, which refers to Annex II, Chapter I (4) of CD 90/667. 19

To the competent authorities of Ireland The monitoring survey for Fireblight should continue to be carried out in the future. The competent authorities of Ireland should consider imposing quarantine measures on plants in nurseries with a possible link to an outbreak and presenting a plant health risk, with the aim to enable a sufficiently long observation period before such material can be moved. This should be supported by changes to existing Irish legislation, to allow their effective operation. The competent authorities of Ireland should inform the Commission in writing of the possible amendments to the legislation in response to the present recommendation within three months of receipt of the final report5.

To the Commission Services The status of protected zone in respect of Erwinia amylovora should be extended beyond 31 March 2000. A strengthening of the Community legislation related to the handling of outbreaks within protected zones, might help the Member States' competent authorities in their search for an stronger legal basis for quarantine measures to be imposed in the case of an outbreak. Such possible new Community legislation should be discussed in relation to the provisions put in place for the production of Fireblight host plants in the buffer zones. 5 See comments from the Irish authorities. 9

recommendations.text: The competent authorities of Ireland should rectify without delay the deficiencies found in the different establishments visited and referred to under the different conclusions in Section 5 above.
The competent authorities of Ireland should take appropriate measures to rectify any deficiencies of the same type found during this mission in all the other approved establishments in Ireland.
The competent authorities of Ireland should address the weaknesses in the supervisory systems at the different levels.

Within three months after the receipt of the final report the competent authorities of Ireland should inform the Commission of the progress and result of the measures taken including a timetable for completion of measures and actions still outstanding at that time. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)1236/1999 Competent Authority's (CA) response to the recommendations in the report The CA has stated, in their letter of 7 February 2000, that the deficiencies noted in the establishments visited during the FVO inspection have been brought to the attention of the management. PAGE 23 1008/03/00 - 35787 In two plants with serious defects, many of those have been rectified, while correction of structural defects is due for completion by June 2000. The action taken for those two plants have been notified earlier to the FVO in detail. The CA stated also to have the intention, in the course of a 3 month review, to issue a progress report for all plants visited by the FVO together with an update on the administrative amendments which were put in place to address the defects noted in the draft report. The Commission services should be informed about such a programme by 31.10.1999, including deadlines for it.

A system of identification of sheep in compliance with Community requirements should be initiated in Ireland without delay to remedy the non-compliances described in point 5.3.5. The Commission services should be informed about measures to be taken by 31.10.1999, including deadlines for these measures.

Immediate action should be taken to remedy the deficiencies with regard to drawing up route plans (described in points 5.3.3. and 5.3.4.) ­ in co-operation with other Member States, if necessary. The Irish authorities should inform the Commission services about measures taken by 30.9.1999. 8.2. To analyse the information about the inspections, the results of the official sampling of the final product and the data on food-borne diseases and zoonoses related to milk and milk-based products in order to apply risk assessment for the prioritization of the food safety activities in the framework of Directive 92/46/EEC.

To ensure that the control of residues of veterinary drugs and contaminants is reinforced in the official sampling programmes as well as in the own checks of the establishments.

To start the process of accrediting the laboratories carrying out testing of official samples of milk and milk-based products as requested by 7 See comments of the Irish competent authorities. 22 Council Directive 93/99/EEC on the subject of additional measures concerning the official control of foodstuffs, supplementing Council Directive 89/397/EEC on the official control of foodstuffs.

To submit a report on the adjusted method for calculating the SCC in cow's milk (Commission Decision 96/360/EC).

Central Competent Authority The Food Safety Authority of Ireland in order to ensure a uniform implementation of the relevant EC legislation, and according to its "mandate" should take action in order to lay down written procedures and guidelines for the "field" inspectors so to enable them to carry out their duties in an uniform way all over the national territory. Additional staff should be appointed, in the framework of the ongoing recruitment procedure, to the contracted/delegated competent authority at central level (DMNR).
Legislation A systematic information procedure, with respect to amendment of the relevant EC legislation, from the central competent authority to the field inspectors should be set up.

Laboratories and residue monitoring programme Action should be taken to ensure that official tasks are executed in a timely and efficient manner and that anonymity of samples analysed is preserved. Samples taken for the residues monitoring programme should be analysed, as soon as possible after their arrival in the laboratory, in order to enable the competent authority to react effectively in case of detection of illegal/incorrect treatments. The laboratory records should distinguish clearly between official analyses and own-checks analyses. Samples for substances of group A of the Annex to Directive 96/23/EC should be taken at all stages of farming.

Inspection of Establishments/Establishments visited The deficiencies concerning standard of operating hygiene in the establishments visited by the FVO inspection team, should be rectified. A programme for re- inspection of the approved premises should be drawn up by the competent authority in order to take similar actions, where necessary, in the establishments not visited during the present mission. Own-checks by plant management - HACCP system - Own checks on water, namely microbiological analyses, should be carried out accordingly to Council Directive 80/778/EEC, in the approved establishments. 14 - Own checks on products, namely microbiological analyses, should be carried out for validation purposes of the HACCP plans, in the approved establishments. Official supervision - Inspection activities should be followed by adequate reporting procedures. Inspection reports should be sent systematically to the hierarchy and to the plant's management. - Official sampling of fishery products for laboratory tests should be carried out in all approved establishments in order to verify the validity of the own- checks programmes. - The HACCP plans should be re-assessed by the competent authority and the re-assessment should be documented. - A revision of the medical certificates should be undertaken, in order to prevent persons liable to contaminate fishery products, from working or handling them. This revision should be reflected in a correct wording of the medical certification.

Auction markets/centres visited and fishing vessels The auction centre visited which was found to be poorly maintained and in generally unsatisfactory condition should be upgraded in order to meet the relevant National and Community requirements. A re-inspection programme of the registered premises should be prepared and executed in order to take similar corrective action, if necessary, in the auction centres not visited by the inspection team. The programme mentioned under § 5.6. (random inspections for vessels of less than 10 metres in length) should be drawn up by the FSAI and the whole fishing vessels fleet should be brought in conformity with the requirements laid down by Council Directive 92/48/EEC.
Fish farm visited A codification of the stunning/slaughtering procedure should be put in place. The hygiene standard of operating procedures related to slaughtering should be improved.

Written guarantees Written guarantees should be forwarded to the European Commission services, including a detailed timetable for the necessary corrective actions, not later than six months, after receiving the final report. 7.2. To the Commission Services To consider drawing up guidelines for the competent authorities carrying out the inspection of fishery product premises, including assessment of HACCP based control systems, and fishing vessels. 15 ADDENDUM TO THE MISSION REPORT DG SANCO/1143/2000 Answer of the competent authority to the recommendations of the report The Irish competent authority has responded to the recommendations of the report. Their comments will be published with the final report on the Internet site of the Directorate General Health and Consumer Protection. Compliance with on-farm burial provisions should be monitored and further enforced to ensure that the probability of unlicensed burial being detected and sanctions being imposed is increased up to a level, which discourages illegal 38 The Irish Authorities have provided comments on this point (see attached annex) 28 disposal of bovine animals. The Competent Authority should investigate the ultimate fate of the large number (circa 27.000) bovines, which cannot be accounted for within the existing movement control system39.

Anamnestic data (or lack of anamnestic data) should be used as a basis to include animals that are being issued a burial licence in the BSE monitoring programme. The Competent Authority should consider sampling a fixed proportion of these animals for BSE examination.

Further training and monitoring of DVOs and practitioners should be arranged to guarantee a high level of vigilance in all counties in order to ensure that the positive trend observed in passive surveillance activities continues.

Export approved slaughterhouses should be closely monitored to guarantee that the instructions on sampling of casualties are followed in all of these plants. 7.1.2. SRM 1. The Competent Authority should consider methods to reconcile incoming and outgoing material in the dedicated SRM rendering plant 2. The Competent Authority should ensure that reconciliation of SRM consignments is carried out properly at all slaughterhouses. 3. The procedures as regards applying health marks to carcasses should be reviewed to ensure compliance with Council Directive 64/433/EEC, in particular: ü Carcasses without health marks shall not be allowed to leave the slaughtering premises. 7.1.3. Feed-ban 1. Risk-based targeting should be adopted in the control and sampling program for feeding stuffs, in particular in the sampling program for controlling the compliance with the feed ban. 2. Controls on the feed ban should be extended to home compounders. 7.1.4. Other 1. All of the cutting plants, including small-scale plants should be approved according to Council Directive 64/433/EEC and supervised by official veterinarians. 39 The Irish Authorities have provided comments on this point (see attached annex) 29 ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT 1304/2000 Competent Authority response to the recommendations in the report The Irish authorities announced in their written comments that they would take the following actions in relation to the recommendations: 1. Risk-based targeting in the control and sampling program for feeding stuffs is being implemented. 2. A total of 200 home compounders are now targeted for sampling. Up to the beginning of the FMD crisis, 83 were sampled and sampling will re-commence after the crisis is over. 3. There are now systems in place to ensure that proper ante-mortem records are kept at all plants, using the CMMS printout to standardise them. 4. Cross-checks between raw SRM intake and yield of MBM and tallow (reconciliation) is now being implemented.
Annual reports under Regulation (EC) No 2630/97 were submitted in February 2001.

An instruction was sent (on 26 February) to all District Veterinary Offices to sample all fallen stock over 30 months of age and at least 20% of bovine animals over 30 months of age for which burial licence have been requested.
Up to the end of April 2001, a total of 2457 fallen stock have been sampled throughout the country (in 36 out of 45 knackeries).

The fallen animal collection service, which will be subsidised by the State, will require accurate and verifiable data on numbers of animals collected to be supplied by the knackeries. Each animal collected by a collector must be reported to ALF in order for the collector to receive the State payment. This should ensure that each animal collected is reported. Also, by reducing the cost to the farmer to a low level, it will be cheaper to have the animal collected than to bury it. Burying of animals will be prohibited except in remote areas and the issuing of burial licences will stop.
Reconciliation of SRM consignments is carried out at slaughterhouses. 30

recommendations.text: The accuracy of the report and working document Comments related to factual inaccuracies have been included in the text of the report. A copy of this section is published on the SANCO Internet site, together with the final report.

The action plan initiated in response to the mission's findings The action plan resulting from the FVO mission established actions to be undertaken during 2001 and 2002. A copy of this section is also published on the SANCO Internet site, together with the final report. 3. The actions taken since the mission 4. Additional information These two latter sections explain in detail the action plan, implementation, measures and procedures as well as further medium-term actions. 29

As regards the casualties, the Irish Authorities should · determine how and where animals which were formerly sent as casualties at the slaughterhouses are being disposed of in order to be satisfied that these animals do not cause any problem to public health and, where relevant, are included in the monitoring programme. · put in place appropriate action to ensure that casualties detected at the ante- mortem examination in the slaughterhouses are sampled in order to comply with Art.1-1 of Commission Decision 2000/764/EC

The Irish Authorities should investigate the reasons for the wide variation in the level of epidemiosurveillance between the DVOs (detection of clinical suspects, sampling in knackeries and of fallen stock issued with a burial licence), and inform the Commision of the outcome of the investigation and the actions taken subsequently;

The Irish authorities should reinforce the controls on the Laboratory carrying out the rapid tests, in order to improve the supervision foreseen in Art.5-1 of Commission Decision 98/272/EC and Art.3-3 of Commission Decision 2000/764/EC as amended

As regards the fallen stock, the Irish Authorities should : · ensure that their sampling is made on a random basis, is representative for each region and continuous as foreseen in Annex I-A-2 of Commission Decision 98/272/EC; in order to ensure the random basis, the official provision not to sample fallen stock without proper animal identification should be reconsidered; 36 · improve their disposal system (as a matter of urgency in the counties where no knackeries are working) in order to be able to have access to all relevant dead animals and to sample them on a random basis (according to the current EU legislation) or to ensure that all animals aged over thirty months are sampled (present national rules), · improve their disposal system in order to improve the quality of the samples taken; whatever the test used, the Competent Authority should consider assessing the reliability of its results when the presence of the specific region of the brainstem (obex) can not be ensured by the sample-taker and/or the laboratory staff due to the autolysis (e.g. comparison with immunohistochemistry results), · establish an adequate monitoring of the performance of the Divisional Veterinary Offices, to ensure that any deficiencies of the control system can be promptly detected and rectified. 8.2 With regards to the feeding of processed animal proteins (1) In the plants authorised for using fish meal, the competent authority should ensure the complete separation (i.e.: from the intake bins to the delivering trucks) of the production lines as laid down in Annex I, point 6, second indent of Commission Decision 2001/9/EC. (2) The competent authority should target inspections and issue instructions to ensure that requirements for production in the feed mills of compound feedstuff containing derogated processed animal proteins and the use on farms are fulfilled. The competent authority should consider taking measures to ensure that reporting of inspections also covers the other checks carried out. (3) The competent authority should ensure that requirements for labelling feedingstuffs containing fishmeal are met as laid down in Annex I, point 7 of Commission Decision 2001/9/EC. (4) The competent authority should designate the official service in charge of control on licensed farms using fishmeal and check effectiveness of channelling of fish meal on the farms.

The competent authority should intensify sampling for microscopic analysis on the farms and in the feed mills taking into account the possibility of cross- contamination prior to and after the use of derogated processed animal proteins. The competent authority should also improve availability of the laboratory results to the local officials and operators concerned and take appropriate follow-up actions in the case of positive samples.

The competent authority should supplement the relevant documentation to ensure that all parts of animals purchased for destruction are rendered and should ensure their full destruction by way of incineration or any other appropriate means as laid down in Article 5 of Commission Regulation (EC) 2777/2000.

The competent authority should transpose Community rules concerning approval requirements for feeding dicalcium phosphate and hydrolysed proteins derived 37 from fish, feather and hides and skins to certain farmed animals as laid down in Commission Decisions 2001/9/EC and 2001/165/EC or to make sure that these products are effectively not used in Ireland. 8.3 With regards to Specified Risk Material (1) The Irish authorities should involve the knackeries in SRM controls, (2) The FSAI should consider extending the ongoing audit in abattoirs and butcher shops supplying the national market, (3) The Irish authorities should improve the system of collection and destruction of fallen stock in order to comply with Commission Decision 2000/418/EC (see also 8.1.4.2nd and 3rd bullet points), (4) The Irish authorities should ensure that SRMs produced in non-export slaughterhouses are collected and disposed of effectively. 38 ADDENDUM In their comments to the draft report, the Irish authorities explain that some recommendations have been already addressed partially or completely (see relevant footnotes in the text): epidemio-surveilla s 8.1.(2), (3), and (4) feeding of processed animal protei s 8.2.(3), (4), (5) and (7) specified risk materials: recommendations 8.3.(3). They indicate too that due to the implementation of Commission Regulation (EC) No1248/2001 on 1/7/2001, many of the recommendations of the draft report have been implemented, especially in relation to active surveillance of fallen animals. 39

recommendations.text: The Irish authorities have indicated that they will provide a detailed report of actions taken by FSAI and DAFRD after receiving the final report.
The Irish authorities also underlined that a series of actions has already been taken arising from the mission.

Separate responses were received from the DAFRD and the FSAI on the draft report. These appeared to reflect differing perception of the roles and responsibilities of the two authorities in this sector. This question will be pursued by the Commission's Services in following up this mission.
Further clarification is being sought with the Commission's Legal Service as regards the transposition of Annex B, Chapter IV of Council Directive 77/99/EEC.

The Irish authorities indicated that in their view, the mission report, in questioning the effectiveness of the controls and monitoring systems operated by the FSAI over food production in the evaluated sectors, goes beyond its remit. The FVO cannot accept any attempt to constrain its ability to evaluate food safety controls in the interest of consumer health protection. The FSAI has an overarching responsibility for food safety controls, elements of which have been formally attributed to the DAFRD. It is essential that the manner in which the FSAI operates, and in which it monitors the activities of its contracted agents, is subject to evaluation by the FVO, if a complete picture of the situation in Ireland is to be given. 24
To maintain appropriate controls to prevent the introduction of FMD into Ireland

Generalities related to CA FP/LBM control system performance As recommended in the previous mission report all relevant legislation should be fully and properly implemented and enforced by the DCMNR. In order to achieve this goal, the setting up of the announced Specialised Food Safety Unit and the compatibility of the food safety and fisheries control duties dedicated to SFOs should be considered as a priority. Additionally, the programmed increase of the number of qualified staff should continue. The formalisation/documentation of corrective actions and procedures ­ namely those already drafted and distributed to SFOs ­, and in particular in relation to report issuing, should be improved. The deficiencies noted in laboratories carrying out analyses for official and private purposes, including those deficiencies identified by the audits already performed by the FSAI, should be corrected. The DCMNR should check all registered fishing vessels and in particular a solution should be found for the inspection of the factory vessel. The Irish authorities should ensure that the conditions applied to imports of fishery products from the USA (included in part II of the list of Annex to Decision 97/296/EEC) are at least equivalent to those governing the production and placing on the market of Community products, in accordance with Article 11.7 of Directive 91/493/EEC. Drinking water should be used within the meaning of Directive 98/83/EC. Its chlorination should be carefully followed by establishments' staff and assessed by SFOs in order to prevent any possible risk for public health. All deficiencies/shortcomings observed in the establishments visited during the mission should be corrected and the CA should ensure appropriate follow up. This also applies to other establishments where similar situations could be found. 21

Live Bivalve Molluscs The MI should put in place their newly drafted working programme in order to comply with the requirements of Directive 91/492/EEC and of Commission Decision 1999/313/EC. The implementation of these requirements should include the correction of the deficiencies identified in 2.2.1 Laboratories of this report. The use of alternative methods for the detection of Saxitoxin (PSP) - different from the biological testing method - should only be considered after its recognition, in accordance with the procedure laid down in Article 12 of Directive 91/492/EEC. The use of alternative chemical methods for the detection of lipophilic toxins - different from the biological testing method - should be considered only after availability of standards for new analogues of public health significance and validation of its performance characteristics following an internationally agreed protocol, in accordance with the requirements of Commission Decision 2002/225/EC. The monitoring for ASP in wild scallops, in particular the transfer of responsibilities from the DCMNR to the private sector should be reviewed according to the requirements of Commission 2002/226/EC. The Irish authorities should undertake the necessary actions in dispatch/purification centres which are not in compliance with the relevant Community requirements. In particular, inspections of dispatch/purification centres, at regular intervals, should be put in place by the Irish authorities, in particular to check the performance of end product testing in accordance with Chapters V of Council Directive 91/492/EEC, and to control establishment own-check HACCP plans developed in accordance with Council Directive 93/43/EEC.

recommendations.text: Ensure that supervision of CBs is adequate to guarantee that controls carried out by CBs are effective, as required by Article 27(9)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. In particular, ensure that: In order to evaluate the operational performance of CBs, as required by Article 92c(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, dedicated staff be allocated to the supervision of the processing activities; All non-compliances found in the performance of CBs are reported to CBs in a timely manner and corrective measures required from CBs, for the CBs to fulfil the requirement of Article 27(8) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. CBs not based in Ireland are equally supervised by DAFM, taking into account all relevant information including reports issued by Accreditation Bodies of the countries where the CBs are based, as required by Article 92(c)(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. This

citations.text: There are six administrative staff in the Organic Unit assisted by two inspectors and one technical officer charged with, inter alia, organic controls of organic production. In addition, there are 30 technical officers who undertake controls at local markets and retailers. All DAFM staff met by the audit team were experienced in the area of organic production and were found to be knowledgeable for the tasks assigned. DAFM staff attend regular training on organic production and meetings, including the Committee on Organic Production held in Brussels. However, DAFM informed the audit team, that due to the limited resources, no dedicated staff member is allocated to supervisory activities in the area of processing.

A system of controls is in place in accordance with Article 27(4) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. CAs responsible for controls in organic production are designated with a clear distribution of tasks and responsibilities among the CAs and the delegated CBs. There is good communication and co-operation between the different CAs, and regular meetings are held between DAFM and the CBs. However, due to limited staff resources, the CA does not adequately supervise CBs controls in the area of processing which reduces the effectiveness of the system in place (see also conclusion no 23). 5.2.1.1 Control Bodies: Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal Legal Requirements Articles 5(2) and (3) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Articles 27(5) to (9) and (14) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92(c) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

Furthermore, as these CBs do not have a branch office in Ireland, the office audits are carried out at the home of the CBs´ inspectors, where all information necessary for supervision might not be available. Moreover, DAFM does not notify the result of the supervision to the CB headquarters, but only to the inspector. Therefore it cannot be ensured that the management of the CB is aware of any non-compliance and that effective corrective measures are taken as necessary.

In addition to office audits, DAFM carries out witness audits to observe the performance of the CBs´ inspectors. According to the information provided to the audit team, eight witness audits were carried out in 2015 at farm level. No witness audits were carried out to observe the performance of controls at processors. The inspections at processors by CBs observed by the audit team were overall superficial and not all relevant requirements were checked by inspectors (see finding 54). The failures in the performance of CBs were not identified by DAFM inspections described in paragraph

The audit team reviewed a number of reports issued by DAFM following witness audits and re-inspections. Several shortcomings were identified and the overall performance of inspectors was evaluated. The shortcomings were notified to the CBs concerned with a delay of several months. This delay in the communication of the results of supervision undermines its effectiveness, as it does not ensure that corrective action is taken by CBs in a reasonable time.

Moreover, corrective measures proposed consisted only in re-inspecting the operator where the supervision had taken place. No corrective measures were proposed by DAFM to or required from CBs to avoid the repetition of the shortcomings related to the performance of the inspectors. Some of the shortcomings described in the reports issued by DAFM were repeated during the inspections observed by the audit team (e.g. no identification of individual animals present on the fields, no measurements of stables in every inspection). The lack of corrective action to address the root cause of the problem detected does not fully ensure the effectiveness of the controls carried out by CBs. This is not in line with Article 27(9)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Conclusions on Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal of Control Bodies

There is a system of approval, annual supervision and withdrawal of CBs in place in Ireland, which includes the withdrawal of the CB's approval by the CA in case a CB fails to fulfil its obligations. Regular coordination and communication between CAs and CBs is established aiming at harmonising organic controls. The effectiveness of the CA's supervision of CBs is however reduced because the CA does not effectively supervise CBs' controls in the area of processing (due to staff shortage). The system is further weakened by the fact that the CA does not take all relevant information into account when supervising CBs located outside Ireland and that several systematic shortcomings in the performance of CBs related to the planning of controls and the enforcement of organic rules were overlooked by the CA during supervision of CBs. Inappropriate communication of such shortcomings by the CA to the CBs hampers timely implementation of appropriate corrective actions. 5.2.2 Registration of operators Legal Requirements Articles 28(1), (2) and (5) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. recommendations.text: Ensure that operators not covered by the exemption provided for in Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 submit their undertakings to the control system, as established in Article 28(1) of the same Regulation. This

citations.text: According to DAFM, Ireland requires the registration of operators as indicated in Article 28(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Any operator who produces, prepares, stores, places organic products on the market or import/export from/to non-EU countries shall submit his undertaking to the control system. Subcontracted operators are also subject to the control system. The audit team reviewed the agreements for the delegation of tasks signed between DAFM and the CBs and noted that the requirement regarding operators who place products on the market was not explicitly included. The audit team noted that wholesalers dealing only with pre-packed and labelled feed were not subject to the control system. In addition, CBs did not adequately verify the activities carried out by traders dealing with pre-packed and labelled food, who were found by the audit team to trade products not included in the scope of their registration certification (see finding 64). This is not in line with the abovementioned Article 28(1).

Since 2012, the Horticulture and Plant Health Division is responsible for inspections at retailers (which were previously inspected by technical staff of the Agricultural Environment and Structure Division). The fulfilment of conditions for the exemption of retailers from official controls is usually checked during these inspections. However, the audit team noted that the scope of these inspections focus on plant production only, and do not cover products of animal origin, providing information to the CA which is insufficient to satisfactorily assess whether retailers exempted under Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 (continue to) fulfil conditions for exemption.

The system however does not ensure that all operators, in particular wholesalers, are registered. Moreover, the fact that the list of operators does not include all required information and is not regularly updated, reduces the tool's functions for effective verification of the status of organic operators.

Although the CA conducts inspections at retailers to verify fulfilment of conditions for exemptions of retailers from organic controls, the limitation of the inspection scope to plant products only, fails to ensure that all relevant retailers are covered by the CA inspections. 5.2.3 Planning and Prioritisation of Controls Legal Requirements Articles 3, 41 and 92f of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the 9 Council. Article 27(3) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Articles 65(1), (4) and 92(c)(2) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

These procedures will be introduced in 2017 and operational immediately after introduction. In relation to operators selling feed (as distinct from food) which was an issue raised during the audit, our review of the legislation leads us to believe that such operators may also be exempt under the terms of Article 28(2) where definition of `products' includes feed, and where a `user' as distinct from a `consumer' is also clearly envisaged. recommendations.text: Ensure that risk analysis carried out by CBs are adequate to provide the basis for determining the intensity of unannounced or announced annual inspections and visits, as required by Article 92c(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. In particular, ensure that: time allocated for inspections to processors is proportionate to the risk of the operator and the announced inspections scheduled at a time when organic products are processed; quantities produced by operators are taken into account as a risk criterion, as required by Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008; the selection of operators to be submitted to unannounced inspections is determined on the basis of risk analysis and that these are planned according to the level of risk, as required by Article 92c(2) (b) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Tis

citations.text: However, the time allocated to inspections at processor level is very limited, even in the case of processors handling large quantities of organic and conventional products. As observed by the audit team during the inspections, not all relevant requirements were checked by inspectors and not all premises were fully inspected, which is not in line with the procedures of the CBs (see finding 54). In addition, CB2's procedures require inspectors to observe the production lines during the production of an organic product once every three years, which means that inspections are not always scheduled to allow verification of conditions under which processing of organic products takes place. This is not in line with Article 92c(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, which requires that results of the risk analysis must provide the basis for the planning of announced and unannounced inspections.

However, CB1 does not take into account for the risk analysis, the quantities produced by operators, which is a compulsory criterion according to Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. In addition, the results of the risk analysis carried out by CB1 and CB2 do not serve in practice as an adequate basis for the planning of annual and unannounced inspections (less than 10% of operators are differentiated by this method). In the case of CB1, the majority of operators were classified in the lowest risk category, while only 2.5% of operators were classified by CB2 as high risk operators. This is not in line with Article 92c(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

The audit team reviewed the list of operators selected by CB1 and CB2 for additional controls, and noted that only a small number of operators visited were selected based on their risk category. CB1 and CB2 carried out most of the additional inspections to new 11 operators and also to follow-up on non-compliances detected during the previous annual inspection. This is not in line with Article 92c(2) (b) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Conclusions on Planning and Prioritisation of Controls

Generally, CBs plan and prioritise controls of operators at a sufficient frequency, including unannounced inspections. However, the effectiveness of the system is reduced as CBs do not consider the quantity of products handled per operator in their risk evaluation and high risk operators are not necessarily subject to additional controls.

While inspections at farm level are generally allocated with sufficient inspection time, there is a risk for inspections at processors to remain rather ineffective as allocated inspection time per operator is too short to allow adequate verification of relevant requirements and / or inspections are not always conducted when organic products are processed. 5.2.4 Controls of operators Legal Requirements Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council. recommendations.text: Ensure that the documented procedures use by CBs are detailed, as required by Article 27(6) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, and, in particular, that checklists used by inspectors include to verify: records kept by operators showing the results of verification at reception of the organic products purchased, as required by Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008; all sites where aquaculture animals are kept, as required by Article 67(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, and records relating to animals kept and quantities of feed used, as required by Article 79(b) of the said Regulation; the conditions under which operations on the management of animals referred to in Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 are carried out by operators. This 25

citations.text: However, the checklists used are not sufficiently detailed and do not include some relevant requirements of EU Regulations. This lack of detailed documented procedures is not in line with Article 27(6)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. During the inspections observed, the audit team noted that inspectors did not check certain requirements that were not included in the checklists, in particular: CBs do not require operators to keep records on the results of verification on reception of organic products as required by Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and do not adequately check records. The audit team noted that the records kept by both processors visited were not designed to verify the organic status of the products purchased, as they lacked relevant information on the labels and delivery notes or invoices (see finding 62). It was noted during the inspection that a processor had been using an ingredient not labelled as organic for the production of an organic product, as no verification had been made on reception by the operator. CB3 does not physically inspect and carry out documentary checks of all sites where aquaculture animals are kept, in particular, records relating to animals kept and quantities of feed used. This is not in line with Articles 67(1)(a) and 79(b) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2009; CB1 and CB2 do not require operators to record the conditions under which operations such as disbudding, dehorning and castration of animals are carried out 13 (see finding 76). The audit team noted that farmers carried out these operations at the most appropriate age, but without applying any anaesthesia or analgesia, which is not in line with Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

The effectiveness of controls at operators was however reduced as checklists used were incomplete and relevant requirements sometimes incorrectly and/or superficially verified by CB inspectors. This concerned in particular inspections at processors where relevant premises were not always fully checked by CB inspectors and stock and financial records not sufficiently verified when performing the calculation of the input/output balance. 5.2.5 Controls on Labelling and Traceability Legal Requirements Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council. Articles 23, 24 and 27(13) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Title III of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

citations.text: Inspections witnessed by the audit team at processors were overall superficial with no in-depth verification of all information provided by operators The following aspects were not adequately checked by inspectors: not all premises were checked by inspectors, even though the CB´s procedures indicates that all premises of an operator must be inspected. The lack of adequate verification of premises is not in line with Article 67(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. CBs did not systematically verify the results of operators´ own quality assurance programs referred to in Article 67(1)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Although the checklist used by CB2 included a specific question on the checks carried out by operators themselves, the inspector did not check any record but simply asked the question to the operator in order to fill in the checklist. The CBs did not provide any evidence to the audit team that this verification has been done in previous inspections. Without this check, CBs cannot verify operators´ compliance with Article 91(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, which requires operators to notify CBs of any non-compliant product that they may have produced or received from third parties. inspectors verified a number of labels in the office of the operators but they did not verify the labels applied to the final products stored in the premises. Moreover, inspectors do not cross-check whether the labels used by operators are still the ones which were approved by CBs . when checking the balance between input and output required by Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, the CBs did not check a representative number of invoices to verify the accuracy of the records kept by operators. In addition, inspectors checked the internal records corresponding to one day of production only, although the CBs´ procedures require inspectors to check the balance input/output of at least one week of production. No other checks were carried out by CBs on stock or financial records kept by operators to verify the nature and quantities of products purchased, produced, stored or sold by operators, which is not in line with Articles 66(1)(a) to (d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. No other documentary checks are carried out during the year, as CBs do not require operators to regularly submit information on their activities. 14 Conclusions on Controls at Operators

The effectiveness of controls at operators was however reduced as checklists used were incomplete and relevant requirements sometimes incorrectly and/or superficially verified by CB inspectors. This concerned in particular inspections at processors where relevant premises were not always fully checked by CB inspectors and stock and financial records not sufficiently verified when performing the calculation of the input/output balance. 5.2.5 Controls on Labelling and Traceability Legal Requirements Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council. recommendations.text: Ensure that labelling and traceability checks carried out by the CA and CBs adequately verify that: operators require documentary evidence of their suppliers including the type or range of all products handled by operators, as required by Articles 29(1) and (2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007; labels applied on final products are those approved by CBs and that they bear all necessary compulsory indications of Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007; the organic nature of the products and where relevant lot numbers are indicated on the documents accompanying the products supplied, as required by Articles 31(1)(b) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008; only products or ingredients which can be proven to satisfy the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 are labelled as organic, as required by Articles 23(1) and (2) and 27(13) of the same Regulation. This 26

citations.text: According to the CBs´ standards, operators must ensure that products are clearly and accurately labelled in order to comply with all relevant requirements. However, labelling checks at processors carried out by CBs are not effective (see finding 54). As a result, CB1 did not note the use by a processor of a label which had not been approved by the CB. The label used indicated the use of a non-organic ingredient of agricultural origin while in the approved label it was indicated as organic. Furthermore, according to the recipe, the ingredient used was 6.7% of the weight of the product, which is not in line with EU Regulations.

In addition, the audit team noted several non-compliances with Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 concerning the labels (e.g. small size or no presence of the EU logo, ingredients of agricultural origin not indicated as organic, non-use of the code of the CB or of the operator who carried out the last operation on the product, etc.). These non- compliances had not been noted by CBs during controls. 15

Moreover, CBs do not adequately follow-up on the use of non-compliant labels. For example, DAFM notified CB1 of a complaint received from a client regarding a label where the main ingredient was not indicated as organic. CB1 informed DAFM on 12 August 2016 that the operator had been asked to change the label. However, the CB did not require the operator to stop using the non-compliant label. The audit team noted that the label was still used for the production of the same product on 18 August 2016. In addition, the CB did not require the operator to demonstrate the organic origin of the ingredient. There was also no request to evaluate if other products in the range could also be subject to the same labelling problem (which was found to be the case by the audit team during the audit).

However, the audit team noted that the organic nature or the lot number of products supplied was not indicated on all accompanying documents. This lack of relevant information did not permit the linking of raw materials supplied with the accounts of the supplier, who also handled similar conventional products. The lack of this information is not in line with Articles 31(1)(b) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Moreover, in the case of the chicken breast, the documents provided by CB2 were not sufficiently detailed to trace the product throughout all the processing steps (slaughter, cutting, packaging and distribution) and therefore it was not possible to track the product back to the farmer, as claimed on the product package. This is not in line with Articles 23(1) and (2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, as it could not be demonstrated that the products and ingredients advertised as organic had been obtained in accordance with the rules of the Regulation.

In addition, the information on the labels was not supported by the documents kept by operators. In the two multi-ingredient products, the information concerning the place where the agricultural ingredients had been farmed (EU/non-EU agriculture) did not match with the information on the documents provided by suppliers. CBs permit processors to always use the reference to EU/non EU agriculture, regardless of where the agricultural products have been farmed, which is not in line with Article 24(1)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

Moreover, the trader who distributed two of the products was not registered for products of animal origin and CB1 had failed to detect this shortcoming. This also indicates that controls carried out by DAFM at retail level do not ensure that operators verify the documentary evidence of suppliers, which is not in line with Article 29(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. 16 Conclusions on Labelling and Traceability

The system in place provides for a regular verification of labelling of organic products and their traceability by CBs and the CA. However, the system has so far failed to effectively rectify recurrent non-compliances with regard to compulsory labelling requirements, including the list of ingredients. 5.2.6 Sampling and laboratory analysis Legal Requirements Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council. recommendations.text: Ensure that the analytical results of the samples taken are reliable, and, in particular, that: the CA designates the laboratories used by CBs, as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; official samples taken by CBs comprise in all cases three individual samples, as required by EU Regulations and by Articles 12(1) and (2) of statutory instrument 112/2004. This

citations.text: However, the sampling procedure used by CB1 is not in line with horizontal and national requirements. The audit team noted that the CB, in accordance with an "informal" procedure, had taken samples, but not provided for counter samples, which prevents the taking of any enforcement measures against the operator concerned in case of dispute. "Formal" samples are only taken when a first positive result is found or when a suspicion exists. This shortcoming, which is not in line with Articles 12(1) and (2) of statutory instrument 112/2004, had not been noted by DAFM supervision.

DAFM has not designated any laboratory for the testing of organic samples which is not in line with Article 12(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team noted that analytical reports from the main laboratory used by one CB did not indicate whether results presented in the reports related to the limits of detection or the limits of quantification, which is an important quality requirement. This shortcoming had been raised by INAB during the previous audit carried out to the CB, but DAFM did not request the CB the correct this shortcoming.

CBs sampling policy ensure that the required minimum samples are taken based on an appropriate risk assessment of operators as well as provide for sampling in cases of suspicion. Although CBs use accredited laboratories for the testing of organic products, these laboratories are not designated by the CA with the risk that relevant requirements and rules are not defined and hence laboratories results inadequate to provide the basis for the enforcement of organic rules. CB sampling procedures are not always adequate, which could reduce the validity of the testing results. Moreover, CBs do not always take appropriate measures in case of positive samples to identify the reason for contamination, nor do CBs always notify the CA of such cases (see chapter 5.2.9). 5.2.7 Exceptional production rules and other derogations. citations.text: Import controls consist of the verification of the Certificate of Inspection accompanying the consignments. So far, no physical checks on consignments have been carried out by DAFM before they are imported. However, no risk assessment was ever made by the DAFM to justify the absence of physical checks which is not in line with Article 27(3) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. DAFM informed the audit team that new procedures in co-operation with the Customs are being developed, which will require importers to notify DAFM 10 days in advance of the arrival of a consignment and the performance of risk-based physical checks by the Organic Unit.

CBs do not require importers to notify in due time the arrival of consignments to be imported, contrary to Article 84 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Visits and sampling at importers is planned based on risk by CBs, but, as indicated in findings 53 and 54, CBs do not systematically check how importers verify consignments at arrival. Therefore, CBs are not necessarily aware of any non-compliant product received by importers. Moreover, CBs do not always inform DAFM of non-compliances detected at importers, in particular when the operator concerned is not directly responsible for the non- compliance (see finding 85). This information can therefore not been taken into account for the planning of import controls by DAFM. Conclusion on Imports of Products from Organic Production

An import control system is in place in Ireland, consisting of documentary checks adequately carried out by the CA. However, the decision on the nature of controls, in particular to carry out physical checks on imported products, is not based on an assessment of the risk of occurrence of irregularities and infringements. The effectiveness of the system is further reduced due to the fact that importers are not required to notify the arrival of consignments to CBs in due time and non- compliances identified at operators by CBs are not notified to the CA to be taken into account for the CA's planning of import controls. 5.2.9 Measures in cases of irregularities and infringements Legal Requirements Articles 54 and 55(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council. Articles 27(5)(d) and 30 of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Articles 91, 92, 92a and 92(d) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

According to the agreement between CBs and DAFM, when CBs detect severe irregularities, they must inform DAFM immediately. However, the audit team noted that not all severe irregularities are notified by CBs, but only the ones classified as "manifest infringements", which need the agreement of DAFM for suspending the license of the operator concerned. Generally, non-compliances are only notified to DAFM after the procedure of appeal has finished and the certification decision has been confirmed by the CB which is not in line with Article 30(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 requiring immediately notification of such non-compliances. Moreover, analytical results showing the presence of unauthorised substances are not notified to DAFM unless the use of unauthorised substances is confirmed which is contrary to Article 27(5)(d) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 requiring immediate notification even in the likelihood of a non- compliance. When non-compliances are notified, this is often made with a significant delay, which undermines the effectiveness of the measures taken by DAFM. 21

This

citations.text: According to the CBs procedures, actions are taken by CBs in all cases where analytical results show the presence of unauthorised substances. CBs visited confirmed during the office audits that the likelihood of a non-compliance (i.e. detection of a traces of unauthorized plant protection product) is not notified, and even if the non-compliance is confirmed, it is not always notified to DAFM (see finding 85). Conclusions on Sampling

CBs sampling policy ensure that the required minimum samples are taken based on an appropriate risk assessment of operators as well as provide for sampling in cases of suspicion. Although CBs use accredited laboratories for the testing of organic products, these laboratories are not designated by the CA with the risk that relevant requirements and rules are not defined and hence laboratories results inadequate to provide the basis for the enforcement of organic rules. CB sampling procedures are not always adequate, which could reduce the validity of the testing results. Moreover, CBs do not always take appropriate measures in case of positive samples to identify the reason for contamination, nor do CBs always notify the CA of such cases (see chapter 5.2.9). 5.2.7 Exceptional production rules and other derogations. Legal Requirements Article 22(2) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 29 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and Annex IX of the same Regulation. Sections 2 to 4 of Chapter 6 of Title II of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

At the time of the present audit, DAFM had not adopted a catalogue of measures as required by Article 92(d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. At the opening meeting, DAFM presented the audit team with a draft statutory instrument for DAFM to apply 20 sanctions to operators in cases where they are found to commit an offence against the organic regulations. However, this legal act has to do with the role of DAFM regarding monetary sanctions applied to operators, and not with the measures to be applied by CBs.

The Organic Food and Farming Standards classify non-compliances in three categories according to the severity of the non-compliance and the certification decision to be taken (corrective action for deviations not affecting the organic status of the products, de- certification of product for irregularities affecting the organic status of the product and suspension of the operator´s licence for severe infringements or with a prolonged effect). However, the classification is not pre-defined for specific requirements of EU Regulations. In addition, no other measures are pre-defined either by CBs for particular cases of non-compliance. As a result, both CBs decide on a case-by-case basis, which does not ensure consistency in the implementation of the measures taken by individual CBs and among CBs. The audit team noted a number of cases which demonstrated the inconsistency and inadequacy of the measures: CB1 detected at a processor one raw material not labelled as organic, which had been used for the processing of an organic product. Despite this being a non- compliance which may affect the organic status of the product, the inspector reported it as a deviation. In fact, the vast majority of the non-compliances found by CB1 were reported as "deviations", even when the organic status of the product was affected. CB2 reported an irregularity as a severe non-compliance with a prolonged effect which should have been notified as a "manifest infringement" according to the description in the CB procedure. However, no suspension of the licence of the operator was proposed by the CB to DAFM. CB2 required one operator to provide evidence that a non-compliant product had not been sold as organic. However, in other cases CB1 and CB2 did not follow the same approach and they only verify the use of non-compliant products at the next inspection.

According to the agreement between CBs and DAFM, when CBs detect severe irregularities, they must inform DAFM immediately. However, the audit team noted that not all severe irregularities are notified by CBs, but only the ones classified as "manifest infringements", which need the agreement of DAFM for suspending the license of the operator concerned. Generally, non-compliances are only notified to DAFM after the procedure of appeal has finished and the certification decision has been confirmed by the CB which is not in line with Article 30(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 requiring immediately notification of such non-compliances. Moreover, analytical results showing the presence of unauthorised substances are not notified to DAFM unless the use of unauthorised substances is confirmed which is contrary to Article 27(5)(d) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 requiring immediate notification even in the likelihood of a non- compliance. When non-compliances are notified, this is often made with a significant delay, which undermines the effectiveness of the measures taken by DAFM. 21

The system in place does not ensure that adequate and harmonised measures are taken in cases of irregularities and infringements. Although OFIS notifications were timely followed up, there was no evaluation by the CA of the actions taken by the CBs. Moreover, CBs do not always and immediately notify the CAs of irregularities, which is, in particular with regard to severe irregularities, undermining the effectiveness of the actions taken by the CA.

recommendations.text: To raise awareness amongst all actors to avoid this mutilation and prevent causing unnecessary pain and suffering to cattle, as required by Article 3 of Directive 98/58/EC.

citations.text: National legislation on animal welfare is found under the Animal Health and Welfare Act of 2013 which prohibits persons from doing, or failing to do, anything or causing or permitting anything to be done to an animal that causes unnecessary pain, distress or suffering. The Statutory Instruments (S.I.s) regulating the welfare of cattle of dairy farms include: S.I. 311 of 2010 implementing Directives 98/58/EC and 2008/119/EC amongst others; S.I. 225 of 2014 on the prohibition of non-medical tail docking of cattle, as foreseen by Paragraph 19 of the Annex to Directive 98/58/EC; S.I. 107 of 2014 and 127 of 2014 regulating operations and procedures carried out on cattle, as foreseen by Paragraph 19 of the Annex to Directive 98/58/EC.

There were 101 general animal welfare inspections of cattle farms (dairy or beef) in 2013 and 117 in 2014 with, respectively, 81 (80%) and 79 (68%) farms reported in full compliance. In 2013 these inspections also reported mutilations as being the most frequent non-compliance (S.I. 225 of 2014), at approximately a third of the total (10 of 32), while for 2014 mutilation non-compliances were approximately 5% of the total (3 of 61). 16. 181 inspections on conditions for rearing calves were carried out in 2013 and 204 inspections in 2014 with, respectively, 137 (76%) and 133 (65%) farms in full compliance: For 2014 DAFM gave inspectors a specific instruction to continue to check if replacement heifers present at the same farm had been tail-docked; In both years the main non-compliances reported, 50% or more of the total, concerned 'Record keeping' together with 'Buildings and accommodation'; The report for 2014 submitted by DAFM to the Commission includes an analysis on the above non-compliances, as required by Article 8(2) of Decision 2006/788/EC, indicating that they respectively "concerned incomplete records of medicines administered" and "were related to cleansing and disinfection of housing, pens, equipment and utensils, the presence of sharp edges and protrusions likely to cause injury to calves and environmental conditions".

In 2015 there were approximately 1,350 cross compliance inspections (for all types of cattle and species other than cattle as well) that specifically included animal welfare (there are other cross compliance inspections that do not include animal welfare as one of the primary objectives but will include welfare if issues are noted during the controls). Cross compliance inspection detected 60 to 70 animal welfare non- compliances per year between 2012 and 2014. Within these the most frequently detected 6 Regulation (EC) No 1698/2005 (OJ L 277, 21.10.2005, p. 1­40) 11 in bovine animals is mutilation (specifically tail-docking, S.I. 225 of 2014) corresponding to approximately a third of the total. For a first time offence this usually results in a 5% deduction in the single farm payment. The number of mutilation non- compliances detected from 2012 to 2014 remained stable.

The audit team was informed by the CA that farmers performing tail-docking, which was detected during both cross-compliance inspections and the pilot of 2016, claimed that they had done it for hygiene reasons and because they were unaware of the prohibition on tail-docking. The CA informed the audit team that the prohibition on non- medical tail-docking of bovines in the national legislation (lastly S.I. No. 225 of 2014) has been in place since 2003. Conclusions on assurances from competent authority activities on farmer's compliance with legal requirements

The CA is actively involved in measures that improve the welfare of cattle on dairy farms. Official controls provide satisfactory assurances of compliance with animal welfare requirements for cattle in dairy farms. Awareness levels on national legislation prohibiting tail docking are not high and, despite some preventive measures, there is an apparently low but continuing level of the banned practice of mutilation (tail-docking) of dairy cows.

Information on official controls on tail docking is already reported in paragraphs 17 to 24. Bord Bia is the only other actor which uses tail docking as a welfare indicator. The low frequency of this non-compliance is also supported by the negative reaction of the farmer group met by the audit team who, when asked for their opinion, immediately condemned this practice. Conclusions on indicators of animal welfare

Improving trends are perceived in the majority of welfare indicators, particularly those which are being promoted by several actors from the industry. Actions for the management of mastitis, through the control of somatic cell count in milk, are strongest since most actors are addressing this issue. Actions addressing tail-docking are weakest, as they are being addressed by only one actor other than the CA. 15

recommendations.text: Ensure that effective and timely action is taken in the light of audit results, as required by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in order to ensure that official controls achieve the objectives of that Regulation.

citations.text: In DAFM, the audit charters of both VIAU and IAU state that independent scrutiny shall be carried out by the Audit Monitoring Group. In practice, this group is one person: both VIAU and IAU have for a number of years used an external expert to scrutinise and provide feedback on their audit programmes, in particular to ensure that appropriate risks were considered. This same individual is a co-signatory of their audit charters.
While this process adds value to the audit programmes, it does not consider other aspects of the audit process and no particular feedback on these aspects has been received.

SFPA has recognised that some adjustments will be necessary to enable the committee to discharge this newer responsibility: The current audit committee membership was set up before the inclusion of audits conducted in accordance with Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 in its remit. As a result its membership was established with a focus on financial auditing and internal controls. The SFPA representative met by the DG SANTE audit team stated the reinforcement of the committee with additional external members with specific expertise relevant to the internal audit of fisheries control and food safety of fishery products was under discussion; The terms of reference for the committee include assisting the SFPA in fulfilling its responsibilities in relation to oversight of the audit process and advising the SFPA on whether an appropriate regime of internal control is in operation. The terms of reference do not include any reference to the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 nor to the requirements of article 4(6) of that Regulation.

The charter states that its scrutiny should have a particular focus on ensuring that the audit process "is capable of producing objective results and meeting its obligations under Regulation (EC) No 882/2004". At the time of this DG SANTE audit, the terms of reference for the independent scrutiny had been drafted, based on the NAS Network document on Independence and Independent Scrutiny. A suitable individual to carry out independent scrutiny had just been identified and it was intended to finalise the terms of reference with this person over the following weeks.

While all competent authorities have taken steps to ensure independent scrutiny: in two competent authorities the arrangements had only very recently been put in place; in another two competent authorities the arrangements were insufficient to achieve the objectives of the process either because the whole audit process was not included in the scrutiny or because the arrangements for such scrutiny did not involve individuals with sufficient relevant experience in the field of audits conducted in accordance with Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

recommendations.text: To authorise processing plants producing PAP for aquaculture whenever these are not dedicated exclusively to processing non-ruminant ABP, as required by Article 7 and point (c) of Section D, Chapter IV of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, provided that relevant conditions are satisfied.

citations.text: In the same Category 3 processing plant visited, a production line for Category 3 poultry blood has been in operation since November 2017. According to the business operator and from what was described in the relevant part of the operator's HACCP plan, the resulting poultry bloodmeal (a type of PAP) was being dispatched to another Member State to be used for the manufacturing of pet food and feed for aquaculture. However, the audit team noted that the competent authority had not yet given the relevant authorisation for the production of PAP to be used in aquaculture, which is necessary when a processing plant also processes ABP of ruminant origin, as laid down in Article 5 7 in conjunction with point (c) of Section D, Chapter IV of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

With the exception of (the very few) traders, the system of official controls covering producers, storage facilities and transporters of PAP is characterised by a relatively high frequency of inspections, is based on risk criteria, and supported by a comprehensive set 7 of procedures. A relatively high number of samples are also planned to verify that PAP to be used in feed are in line with relevant microbiological criteria and are free from non-authorised proteins of animal origin.
