recommendations.text: To ensure that the official controls in establishments producing RTE food are carried out by SFPA with the planned risk based frequency in line with Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in all regions, and in particular in establishments producing high risk RTE fishery products; to this end, CA should have access to a sufficient number of suitably qualified and experienced staff as required by Article 4, paragraph 2, point (c). of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: All CAs reported a shortage of resources over recent years, which according to the CAs and the internal audit reports seen led to not achieving the target for planned controls and occasionally to reducing the official samples for process hygiene criteria (limited staff at laboratory level as well). All CAs reported progress in hiring new staff after the ban on recruitment of public servants in Ireland was lifted. Currently, most CAs achieve targets above 90% of the planned controls with efforts being made to ensure a swift handover and training of new staff.

In contrast, certain difficulties in this respect are still encountered in SFPA. Figures emanating from the new quantification system (see paragraph 20) indicate that SFPA achieved 71% of the overall planned official controls, and 60% of the controls in high risk RTE food producing FBOs. The figures indicate that the two regions with the 7 highest number of FBOs have the lowest rate of implementation of controls (43% and 57%).

The same quantification system highlights that the FBOs producing high risk RTE fishery products have amongst the lowest rates of implementation of SFPA controls (between 29% and 39%) compared to other types of FBOs in the regions with the highest number of FBOs. The highest rate of implementation of controls concerned FBOs producing low risk non-RTE foods, which was explained by the lower number of scheduled controls. In most cases, FBOs had been subject to controls at a minimum of once per year in 2017, with only a small number of RTE food producing establishments receiving no official controls in 2017

The SFPA resource challenge had been identified by FSAI in a 2016 audit and work has been done to quantify it through the new quantification system, resulting in the data provided in paragraphs 10 and 11, but the corrective action is outstanding. SFPA attributed this to a lack of staff, difficulties in recruiting also due to budgetary constraints as well as the fact that SFPA is undergoing a management reorganisation.

Challenges were identified in particular in relation to the availability of personnel resources, aspects of training and verification of effectiveness of controls. These challenges, together with delays in effectively addressing audit findings which identified some of these issues, may and sometimes do impact on the controls over the production of RTE foods, to a greater extent for SFPA.

The controls are largely implemented by the CAs as planned, with the risk based frequency, mainly without prior warning. However, in the case of SFPA, while the planned frequency of controls in establishments producing high risk RTE fishery products is three times per year, the implemented frequency in 2017 was approximately once per year - the same as for establishments producing low risk RTE - in the regions with the highest numbers of FBOs.

The similar level of implemented controls for all types of FBOs in these two regions, despite having been assigned different inspection frequencies on the basis of identified risks, together with the limited attention given to new approvals in another region (see also paragraph 30) suggest that SPFA, in the face of dealing with limited resource and with multiple tasks may have to look again at the prioritisation process to ensure resource for higher risk facilities within and between regions. 4.4.1.2 Procedures for official controls

SFPA highlighted that the joint controls between SFPA official controls staff support the identification of shortcomings and gave an example of one region where 80% of the inspections are joint inspections. However, in one of the regions with the highest number of FBOs, 1% of the inspections were explained by the CA to be joint inspections. The CA highlighted a constant increase in the number of fishery establishments in the busy regions.

No official control officer was assigned to one of the fishery establishments visited by the audit team. No official controls had been carried out in this establishment in the past year, although three were planned. Several non-compliances were noted on the day of the audit team visit, including some long standing ones.

Each CA has put in place a system of risk based official controls over production of RTE foods, supported by procedures and covering relevant aspects of the legislation. Most establishments producing RTE products are placed in the "high risk" category, reflected in a higher frequency of controls which is largely achieved by the CAs, except SFPA.

recommendations.text: To review the current approval procedures and implementation thereof with a view to ensuring : that conditional approval does not exceed six months, that full approval is not granted before an inspection of the premises under operational conditions, with satisfactory result, and that the approval of establishments is kept under review and FBOs are approved only for the activities they carry out and for which they meet the relevant legal requirements, as required by Article 31, point 2 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The CAs have procedures in place for approval of food business establishments supporting them in ensuring compliance with the provisions of Article 31, paragraph 2 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Examples of CAs following the procedures were presented to the audit team. The FBOs visited during the audit were in most cases approved for the activities they carried out. However, during the visits on the spot the audit team noted that not all CAs ensure systematic compliance with the provisions of the points (c), (d) and (e) of the above mentioned paragraph: a. Contrary to the provisions of point (d), paragraph 2, Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004: i. local SFPA staff granted full approval to one of the two fishery establishments visited by the audit team based on their first on-site visit carried out when the establishment was not in operation. The CA explained that full approval was granted based on compliance with infrastructure and equipment requirements and on confidence with the implementation of FBOs food safety management system in the previous FBO premises. SFPA central level accepted the approach due to resources limitations. The CA saw the establishment in operation only one year later as a result of local prioritisation of tasks at busy times and with limited resources. ii. in one of the two recent cases reviewed by the audit team where SFPA used conditional approval for new FBOs, the establishment operated on conditional approval for longer than the maximum of six months allowed by Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. SFPA at central level highlights to the local inspectors when the approval visits are due, but it does not follow-up by highlighting when the establishments are no longer covered by the conditional approval. b. Contrary to the provisions of points (c) and (e), paragraph 2, Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, i. some of the issues identified in the establishment under LA official control, for example in relation to infrastructure and operational procedures, could have been addressed when the establishment was approved. The LA welcomed FSAI expert support at the time of approval of establishments subject to flexibility rules. FSAI confirmed to be in the position to provide this support. ii. difficulties with staff uniform understanding of the use of approval categories resulted in establishments being approved also for activities they did not carry out and missing an activity carried out. "Drying and salting for consumption" was listed in the approved activities of one 12 establishment under SFPA supervision, where salting was only a step in the production of smoked fish. Production of shrimp cocktail which, according to the CCA, should be within the approved activities was omitted in the approval of the same establishment performing this activity. Despite the lack of availability of cooking equipment in one fishery establishment "Cooking and breaded products" was specified among the approved activities by SFPA as in the past the FBO made trials for such production. iii. Another fishery establishment was approved as a coldstore where the chillers on-site were only used for own production. This establishment was also approved for chowder production which did not take place, because the wider approval category included chowder production. iv. One meat product establishment under DAFM supervision was also approved for minced meat, although mincing was only an intermediary step in the production of meat products for several years. The recent CA approval visit concerned only extension of premises and did not identify that the current approval was not up to date. The approval certificate was amended during this audit to reflect the current activities, but similar findings had been identified also in report of audit DG(SANTE)/2013- 6693 which suggest that the measures put in place following the above mentioned audit had not been fully effective in preventing reoccurrence.

Each CA has a system for registration and approval of establishments producing RTE foods and strives to support compliance within own organisation. The CAs apply the related procedures which for several aspects are supportive of achieving compliance. In some cases, the implementation of the approval procedures does not ensure full compliance with the provisions of Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (SFPA, VPHIS, LA), partially due to training and staffing issues. There is scope for further exploiting synergies and sharing practices through coordination between CAs in order to further strengthen the current procedures.

citations.text: The national guidance issued by FSAI for flexibility within the provisions of the Hygiene Package addresses RTE food production to a very limited extent, and only for the local authorities (LA)s. The other CAs (see paragraph 7) do not benefit from national measures on flexibility. An ad-hoc approach is used by CAs in most-cases.

The visits on the spot demonstrated that implementation of official controls in relation to FBOs flexibility measures in small establishments proves still challenging. The CAs indicated that they would welcome further national support in order to avoid that non- compliances are accepted as flexibility (see paragraphs 47, 54 and 82 g). Conclusions on national measures

There is scope for further exploring the flexibility options allowed by the EU legislation for the RTE sector in the national measures to support a harmonised and correct implementation thereof by the FBO and related official controls.

Coordination and cooperation mechanisms within and between CAs are in place and functioned as expected for the outbreak investigation and food incidents cases evaluated by the audit team. Nevertheless, some of the different approaches taken by CAs, as described under the different chapters of this report, each with strengths and sometimes weaknesses, suggest that sharing the good practices for strengthening each other's systems through coordination is not fully exploited.

Most CAs have laid down criteria of what constitute "significant change in activities" (under Article 6, paragraph 2 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004) that FBOs are required to notify to ensure CAs have up-to-date information on the establishments. This information supports CAs in early detection of changes that impact the approval/registration conditions as well as early detection of non-compliances. However, as each CA developed own criteria, exploiting the potential for synergies between CA through coordination and sharing of practices within and between Agencies, may further enhance the individual approaches. Some examples are presented below: a. Within DAFM, VPHIS requires meat establishments to notify the CAs of major structural changes. This is not the case for Dairy Inspectorate which requires dairy establishments to notify of additions of new processes or new products only. The dairy inspectors enquire with the FBOs if structural changes took place since their last official control and their possible impact on the approval conditions, but this will take place during the visits on the spot when changes may be already in place. b. Some CAs link the approval with the infrastructure capacity of the establishment that ensures adequate operation under hygienic conditions. Others only deal with the non-compliances related to lack of space due to increased production volumes when they are identified at the time of the routine controls. HSE links the approval 13 with a maximum capacity only for activities subject to approval, not for all foods produced in the same establishment. c. In a multi-activities establishment under HSE supervision, the increased volume of work for the production of composite products that did not require approval, led to production in rooms not initially intended for this purpose or not at the capacity noted at the time of the audit and to some unhygienic practices that impacted all types of production (e.g. inefficient cleaning and verification thereof for some fixtures and equipment, unhygienic storage of exposed food contact materials - see also paragraph 76 - and of exposed ingredients on low racks next to the chiller door due to lack of space). Conclusions on registration and approval of food business operators

Each CA has a system for registration and approval of establishments producing RTE foods and strives to support compliance within own organisation. The CAs apply the related procedures which for several aspects are supportive of achieving compliance. In some cases, the implementation of the approval procedures does not ensure full compliance with the provisions of Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (SFPA, VPHIS, LA), partially due to training and staffing issues. There is scope for further exploiting synergies and sharing practices through coordination between CAs in order to further strengthen the current procedures.

The audit team noted different approaches between and in some cases within the CAs in connection to the fact that each has its own procedures. Some of the procedures are more supportive of swiftly achieving compliance than others- for example in relation to approval of establishments, audits of FBOs procedures and practices, the deadlines used for similar type of non-compliances and verification of effectiveness of controls (see paragraphs 40 to 43 and 75 to 77).

All CAs use their enforcement powers when they identify non-compliances, but some of the differences between CAs in assessing the gravity of findings, in the deadlines given for rectifying shortcomings as well as in their procedures for official controls and 23 verifying the effectiveness of these controls, suggest a missed opportunity for exploiting synergies and ensuring a level playing field through coordination, in particular for FBOs of the same sector or with the same risk categorisation.

citations.text: Challenges were identified in particular in relation to the availability of personnel resources, aspects of training and verification of effectiveness of controls. These challenges, together with delays in effectively addressing audit findings which identified some of these issues, may and sometimes do impact on the controls over the production of RTE foods, to a greater extent for SFPA.

Some CAs aim to cover compliance with all legal requirements within two to three years (with two visits per year), while others aim to achieve the same in one year with a range between two to twelve visits per year, depending on the CA. The depth and thoroughness of the controls vary between CAs. The DAFM checklists for HACCP tend to focus on the main activity and due to the infrequency of the marginal activities the related controls focussed on the main production in the small dairy establishments visited. Marginal activities are subject to official sampling and the food safety management system that manages all activities is subject to audit (see also paragraph 47e).

citations.text: FSAI and each of the CAs have audit structures in place to verify the effectiveness of CAs controls. The reports of all FSAI audits are published on their website. The focus given to controls over RTE food production varies between CAs and sometimes it is limited, although the CAs associate the RTE food sector with a higher risk. a. FSAI carried out horizontal scope audits of CAs that included aspects relevant also for the RTE sector. The first and only FSAI audit specifically targeting the official controls over RTE food production took place in 2016. This audit concerned DAFM controls in meat establishments and covered relevant aspects of the performance of these controls. DAFM put in place several corrective actions for the identified weaknesses. b. DAFM latest audits covering this topic had been in 2010 and 2011 and targeted the controls in the dairy sector. The audits focussed on the controls and procedures for assessing FBO compliance with the HACCP requirements and the microbiological criteria as set out in Regulation (EC) No. 2073/2005. Both audits had largely positive outcomes. c. FSAI informed the audit team that specific audits of the official controls exerted in the RTE sector had been carried out in five LAs during 2015 and 2016. The two 9 reports made available to the audit team concluded that the controls were effective in facilities producing RTE meat products. d. HSE and SFPA, organisations with more recent internal audit arrangements, had not carried out internal audits focussing specifically on official controls related to production of RTE foods.

Challenges were identified in particular in relation to the availability of personnel resources, aspects of training and verification of effectiveness of controls. These challenges, together with delays in effectively addressing audit findings which identified some of these issues, may and sometimes do impact on the controls over the production of RTE foods, to a greater extent for SFPA.

All CAs use their enforcement powers when they identify non-compliances, but some of the differences between CAs in assessing the gravity of findings, in the deadlines given for rectifying shortcomings as well as in their procedures for official controls and 23 verifying the effectiveness of these controls, suggest a missed opportunity for exploiting synergies and ensuring a level playing field through coordination, in particular for FBOs of the same sector or with the same risk categorisation.

recommendations.text: Sector specific targets for reducing, refining or replacing antimicrobial use 69. Although there is clear progress in implementing iNAP, there are no targets or other indicators to measure its real impact (in terms of reduction of the use of antimicrobials and the levels of AMR). The competent authority explained that they have considered establishing targets but, in the absence of data on the usage per species, it was deemed unfeasible (52). A recently published study (53) by Teagasc, DAFM and UCD which looked into measures deployed in other Member States to reduce the use of antimicrobials, the use of targets has been recognised as a positive tool to motivate and change the behaviour of veterinarians and farmers. 70. The competent authorities have developed a database to collect the data on the use of antimicrobials at farm level. This database is due to be launched shortly for pigs, and at a later stage for the remaining farmed animals (54). The database will also progressively provide the competent authorities with sector specific usage data, which could be used for establishing the targets. The usage of the database will be obligatory under the new Bord Bia quality assurance scheme for the pig sector (see below). The authorities intend to use the data, among other purposes, to allow farmers to benchmark themselves according to their use of antimicrobials and develop a better understanding of their usage patterns. There are already indications that benchmarking (as part of a pilot project in pig sector, see section 4.3.4.3) has succeeded in reducing the use of antimicrobials among some of the highest users. In the above mentioned study (53), the use of benchmarking in other Member States was recognised as an effective motivational tool for farmers and veterinarians. For competent authorities, the benchmarking allows identification of best practice and 52 In their response to the draft report, the competent authorities noted that there is a lack of data on use of antimicrobials to set usage targets and there was a need to improve education and AMR awareness before setting realistic quantitative targets. The competent authority acknowledged the difficulty to measure iNAP outcome qualitatively and noted that the use of quantitative antimicrobial usage targets for animal health sector will be considered for the next iteration of iNAP. 53 https://www.agriculture.gov.ie/media/migration/animalhealthwelfare/amr/inap/iNAPAnimalHealthIm plementationCommitteeReportProject30011019.pdf 54 In their response to the draft report, the competent authorities confirmed that the database to collect the use of antimicrobials in pigs at farm level was launched on 1 November 2019, and that the databases for the rest of the farmed animals will be launched at a later stage. 26 targeted intervention, when the prescribing and usage pattern deviate significantly from the average. 71. Other drivers for change include pressure from the consumer. Due to welfare concerns, marketing the meat as `antibiotic free' is generally not recommended and the competent authority stated clearly that they will not support such an approach. However, there are already signs that the consumers are interested in buying products produced in line with prudent use principles. One of the biggest retailers has showed interest in obtaining data on the use of antimicrobials at farm level in the pig sector in order to include it in the quality criteria they require from their suppliers. Also six out of the seven main retailers have signed up to a `responsible antibiotic use' initiative run by FSAI, DAFM and Bord Bia.

Availability of veterinary antimicrobials and veterinary care 72. With one exemption, the current legislation (European Communities (Animal Remedies) (No 2) Regulations 2007) allows for any veterinarian to prescribe veterinary medicinal products (VMPs) providing that he or she has sufficient knowledge of the animal or animals to form an opinion of their health status and has visited the farm or the premises where the animals are held sufficiently often and recently enough to have an accurate picture of the health, welfare and disease status of the animals. The legislation also lays down controls regarding what constitutes a real relationship between a veterinarian and farmer and outlines criteria that must be met for an animal to be considered under the care of a veterinarian. The requirement to visit the farm does not apply to the prescribing of an intramammary antimicrobial agent, if the animal belongs to a herd covered by a mastitis control programme meeting the specific requirements laid down in the above-mentioned legislation. This exception is called `Schedule 8' route and requires the prescribing veterinarian to have an up-to-date knowledge of the herd health situation, which could be achieved by consulting the relevant data and reports, but without him or her having to visit the farm. The majority of the dairy cow population is covered by the co- operative mastitis control programmes and the `Schedule 8' prescribing route is used widely. In 2015, 45% of lactation tubes and 51% of dry cow therapy tubes were supplied via `Schedule 8' (55). There are however some positive developments regarding `Schedule 8' route as the co-operatives are no longer stocking intramammary tubes containing CIAs and actively promoting milk recording (56). 55 S.J. More, T.A. Clegg, F. McCoy. The use of national-level data to describe trends in intramammary antimicrobial usage on Irish dairy farms from 2003 to 2015. J. Dairy Sci., 100 (2017), pp. 6400-6413. 56 In their response to the draft report, the competent authorities noted that the majority of mastitis tubes are supplied by private veterinary practitioners and that the DAFM Policy Document on HP - CIAs is driving behavioural change with regard to the prescribing practices around 3rd and 4th generation cephalosporins. The competent authorities also noted that individual co-op figures and the AHI are identifying annual decreases in the relatively high use of intramammary tubes for dairy cows. The adoption of SDCT will also reduce intramammary use over the next 2 years as compliance with the new veterinary legislation will include mandatory adoption of SDCT as part of the new veterinary prescription process. A significant 7% reduction in intramammary tube usage has been achieved over the last 8 years (when corrected for dairy cow population). This will improve further as farmers are now becoming increasingly aware of the benefit of SDCT. 27 73. As one of the actions under iNAP's Strategic Objective 4 ('Optimise the use of antibiotics in human and animal health') the Veterinary Council of Ireland (VCI) recently updated its Code of Professional Conduct in relation to prescribing practices in animals under veterinary care (57). The guidance, complementary to the VCI 'Ethical use of antibiotics' poster (58), is stricter than the legislative requirements. Under the new rules, an antibiotic can only be prescribed if a veterinarian clinically examined an animal or animals in the last 30 days (90 days for other VMPs). In order to prescribe, the veterinarian is also required to have an established, even if informal, client-patient-practice relationship. The Commission team noted that the guidance, goes beyond the current legal requirements (which are either a visit, or using `Schedule 8' provisions). The guidance is not mandatory, however the veterinarians could potentially face disciplinary action over not adhering strictly to the recommended time limits. 74. The VCI requirement of an established veterinarian-client relationship does not preclude multiple veterinarians providing services to the same farmer. In addition to the VCI guidelines, the new Bord Bia Quality Assurance Scheme for the pig sector, due to be introduced later this year, will include a requirement for a farmer to nominate one veterinarian with overall knowledge of herd health. The farmer can use several veterinarians, but the designated one must have overall responsibility for the herd. 75. The above mentioned study on measures implemented by other Member States (53) noted their good experience with connecting veterinarians and farmers in a binding one-to-one relation, with the veterinarian being responsible for the implementation on mandatory herd health and treatment plans and becoming the primary advisor. However, there were concerns aired that any requirement to use one veterinarian will adversely affect the operation of a freely competitive veterinary services market. 76. Another action under iNAP's Strategic Objective 4 was the recent publication of the DAFM policy document on Highest Priority CIAs (HP-CIAs). As there are no national legislative provisions restricting the use of CIAs, this document provides advice on using them as a last resort and a list of VMPs containing CIAs that are available on the market. Apart from being informative, the policy document is meant to support the veterinarians who refrain from using CIAs when pressured to do so by their clients. The restrictions in other Member States on the use of CIAs resulting in significant decreases in consumption of these classes were mentioned in the above mentioned study (40). The future impact of the new EU legislation on VMPs (Regulation (EU) 2019/6 of the European Parliament and of the Council) which come into effect in January 2022 was also considered. It is too early to assess 57 http://vci.ie/getmedia/ba56821b-a76e-4df4-9d10-7319e4fc47a2/VCI-Animals-under-Veterinary-Care- Guidance.pdf?ext=.pdf 58 https://www.vci.ie/Publications/ETHICAL-USE-OF-ANTIBIOTICS-(1) 28 the impact of the policy; however in light of increasing total sales of CIAs more drastic measures might be required (59). 77. Apart from the DAFM policy, a similar message regarding the use of CIAs and antibiotics in general is included in the Code of Good Practice Regarding the Responsible Prescribing and Use of Antibiotics in Farm Animals developed by the Irish Farming Association (IFA), Veterinary Ireland and the Irish Creamery Milk Suppliers Association under the leadership of Animal and Plant Health Association (APHA), the representative body for manufacturers and distributors of animal and plant health products, and with support from other stakeholders and authorities. Although the guidance is rather general, the involvement of a large variety of stakeholders, often with conflicting agendas, must be appreciated (60). The sector specific guidelines are to follow shortly (61). 78. An interesting intervention aimed at reducing the use of HP-CIAs was recently launched by the UCD Veterinary Hospital. The bacteriology laboratory introduced a 2-tier system of reporting of AST results providing only the first choice agents for the particular organism and/or condition. Only if there is resistance with no suitable product for treatment on the primary list, the susceptibility results for agents on the secondary list are released.

Reducing the need for veterinary antimicrobials 79. The representative of the IFA stated that antibiotics are, and will remain, a vital tool for farmers in maintaining and protecting the health and welfare of the animals, and are also needed to produce affordable food. The IFA supports the fight against AMR and encourages its members' efforts to follow best practise in animal husbandry and to use the antimicrobials prudently. One of the biggest poultry processors explained that the poultry industry has already entered a post-antibiotic era and how they have managed to move from routinely medicating each batch of broilers to not using any antimicrobials in over 90% of the birds they currently place on the market. The Commission team was presented with exemplary cases where farmers have managed to eliminate or substantially reduce the use of antimicrobials in different animal sectors. 59 In their response to the draft report, the competent authorities noted that the new VMP Regulation will change the regulatory framework around supply and use of antimicrobials to promote responsible use and it is impractical to try to implement new legislation before then. In addition, the authorities are seeking to strike the correct balance between compulsory and voluntary measures to positively influence antimicrobial prescribing patterns. Progress has been achieved with 13% national sales reduction in 2018 which can improve with industry initiatives on biosecurity and data collection to improve on-farm animal health. 60 In their response to the draft report, the competent authorities noted that DAFM policy is to work in partnership with stakeholders and the process of reaching agreement with diverse stakeholders leads to more effective outcomes. This collaborative approach lays down a framework for future initiatives. 61 In their response to the draft report, the competent authorities noted that the sector specific guidelines for pig and dairy farms were launched at the DAFM and Teagasc AMR and Anthelmintic Resistance Conference in November 2019. 29 80. A pig farmer gave a presentation outlining his 2-year journey from managing a herd with multiple health issues and frequent use of medicated feed to not using any in- feed antibiotics or zinc oxide and lower labour costs. This is in contrast to the heavy reliance of the pig industry on medicated feed due to a lack of investment in water delivery systems which allow for appropriate treatments at the correct dosage and duration (62). 81. A dairy and beef famer focused on reducing the somatic cell count in his dairy herd, with a view to introducing SDCT; with regard to the rearing of calves, he managed to improve husbandry standards with better colostrum management, hygiene, infrastructure and diseases management. All farmers met highlighted the importance of changing the mind-sets and practises, while cooperating with their veterinarians, other advisors and farmers. All agreed that there are substantial costs required to improve farm infrastructure, provide better nutrition and implement comprehensive vaccination programmes. However, the end result is better farm profitability, and improved welfare and performance of the animals. 82. Many of these initiatives are included in iNAP under Strategic Objective 5 ('Promote research and sustainable investment in new medicines, diagnostic tools, vaccines and other interventions') aimed at addressing knowledge gaps concerning links between the health and welfare of animals, as well as with other factors (e.g. farm biosecurity and the use of antimicrobials). The iNAP Animal Health Plan implementation progress reports provide detailed information on many initiatives currently in place. The outcomes or expected outcomes of some projects are highlighted below. 83. Teagasc is carrying out research in relation to mastitis controls and trailing SDCT in several herds based on the results of routine milk recordings. This runs alongside a comprehensive CellCheck programme promoting milk recording and SDCT led by AHI with support from DAFM and EU funded Targeted Advisory Service on Animal Health (TASAH). The programme includes on-farm educational events, co- financed on-farm veterinary consultations and establishment of a 'Partner Laboratories' network overseen by DAFM Laboratories (see 4.3.1). In addition, the dairy processors offer financial incentives for suppliers to promote milk recording, and pledge additional support towards CellCheck veterinary consultation visits. All these initiatives have already contributed in 2019 to an increased number of cows being milk recorded (20% increase over 2018). The goal is that the farmers will have data driven prescriptions for intra-mammary tubes and, as a final goal, will be able to opt out from current blanket use of antibiotics for all cows to dry them off. 84. Other AHI actions under iNAP include the CalfCare project to promote best practice around calving and calf rearing, and the TASAH funded biosecurity assessments of 62 In their response to the draft report, the competent authorities noted that the water based antimicrobial delivery systems are not without their own issues in terms of solubility of antimicrobials in water and precipitation of antimicrobials out of solution and that the targeted feed delivery systems generally reduce use of antimicrobials. 30 pig and, more recently, poultry farms. The results of the pig farms assessed so far show high external biosecurity, mostly due to the type of production, but low internal biosecurity, highlighting the need for better farm husbandry practices. 85. AHI is also running a number of disease eradication programmes (Johne's disease, Bovine Viral Diarrhoea, Infectious Bovine Rhinotracheitis). Additionally, the Beef HealthCheck programme, run in collaboration with DAFM and the industry; provides farmers and their veterinarians with a feedback on the health status of their herds through the provision of the slaughter data. Based on the standard scoring of a set of conditions, the farmers receive online reports of each batch slaughtered. These data allow targeted health interventions such as parasite control, nutrition, vaccination to control losses and to improve the herd health. A similar Pig HealthCheck programme is about to start. These activities are not included in iNAP, but their overall aim is improving the health status of the national herd, which should also result in the reduced use of antimicrobials. 86. UCD and Teagasc, in collaboration with DAFM and other partners, are heavily involved in var

audits.title: Feed additives, their ingredients and traceability

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls are capable of verifying that feed business operators meet their obligations in terms of appropriateness of the retained samples taken, as required by the section "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

citations.text: Relevant guidance documents (see finding 16) contain instructions on controls of retained samples (i.e. those to be taken and kept by FeBOs from ingredients and final 6 products manufactured). The audit team checked some of these samples randomly, and all of these had been appropriately taken, labelled and kept under control in dedicated storage places. These retained samples from feed additives and premixtures were kept at least for six months or until the end of the shelf-life of the products produced with these ingredients. Retained samples of compound feeds were kept at least for three months or until the end of the shelf-life of the produced products. The samples had not been sealed properly except at one FeBO visited. In two compound feed producers visited, retained samples were not taken from amino acids used for production. This is not in line with the requirements of point 4 of Annex II "QUALITY CONTROL" to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Previous inspection reports in these establishments did not mention this non- compliance. 5.2.1.4 Labelling

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. The effectiveness of the inspections is weakened by incomplete verification of the appropriateness of retained samples in compound feed manufacturers and observed shortcomings in officials' verification of the correctness of labelling of feed additives and premixtures particular in relation to products originating from outside of Ireland. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

responses.response: ess - Feed Business Operators will be informed by way of Trader Notice of the requirement to retain samples of additives used in the manufacture of compound feed and of the requirement for all retained samples (ingredients and manufactured product) to be adequately sealed. - Inspection guidance documents and inspection report forms will be updated as necessary to enable verification of compliance - Training will be provided to staff on updated guidance and inspection documents and procedures - Deadline for completion ­ 30/11/19

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls are capable of verifying that feed business operators' labelling satisfies the requirements laid down in Article 3(1)(b) and Article 16 of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003, in particular in relation to feed additives originating from third countries and other Member States.

citations.text: The audit team also checked documentation/labelling of imported feed additives and noted that generally these products fulfilled the relevant authorisation requirements laid down by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003. Some exceptions were identified relating to amino acids (no information on the bacterial strain used). The competent authority had overlooked these non-compliances during previous official inspections.

The audit team noted that, at the FeBOs visited, the labelling control focused on the final products but not on feed additives, premixtures used during the production. At the time of the audit, the audit team identified numerous shortcomings relating to labelling of feed additives/premixtures used as ingredients for production and some shortcomings relating to the labelling of premixtures and complementary feeds produced in the majority of the establishments visited. Most labelling shortcomings related to products originating from outside Ireland and these had been overlooked during previous inspections. Examples of non-compliances included: 7 The functional group of feed additives were missing on the labels of feed additives, which is a legal requirement of Article 16(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003. Safety recommendations regarding the use and/or specific requirements mentioned in the authorisation of the feed additive were not labelled which is a legal requirement of Article 16(1)(e) of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003. Name or business name and address of business/person responsible for the production/import/trade of feed additive was not on the label which is a legal requirement of Article 16(1)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003. The use of certain premixtures containing vitamin A in accordance with the labelled instruction would lead to the established maximum levels of vitamin A in complete feed for fattening pigs being exceeded, which is contrary to the requirements laid down in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 2015/724. Labelling of mixture of feed additives did not contain the approval number of the importer/trader company which is a legal requirement of Article 16(1)(d) of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003 and the word premixture which is a legal requirement of Article 16(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003. Based on a dosage instruction of a complementary feed the daily intake of a feed additive was lower than the minimum required in the authorisation of the additive in Commission Regulation (EC) No 537/2007. Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. The effectiveness of the inspections is weakened by incomplete verification of the appropriateness of retained samples in compound feed manufacturers and observed shortcomings in officials' verification of the correctness of labelling of feed additives and premixtures particular in relation to products originating from outside of Ireland. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

responses.response: ess - Feed Business Operators will be informed by way of Trader (b) Notice to have appropriate control systems in place to ensure that all feed additives and premixtures under their control (including feed additives and premixtures imported from third countries and other MSs) are labelled in accordance with Regulation (EC) 1831/2003 - Inspection guidance documents and report forms will be updated to: (i) incorporate an increased frequency of checks to verify compliance of feed additives and premixtures with labelling requirements under Article 16 of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003 and (ii) to enable the verification that the conditions for use of additives as set out in Regulation 1831/2003 and in the authorisation of the specific additives are met - Training will be provided to staff on updated guidance and inspection documents and procedures - Deadline for completion ­ 30/11/19 Page: 1 port ref. recommendations.text: To ensure that staff carrying out official sampling is provided with necessary information to ensure following the sampling requirements laid down by Article 1 and Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009, specifically for control of substances with non-uniform distributio

citations.text: Local inspectors met had a good knowledge of official sampling requirements laid down in Regulation (EC) No 152/2009 including the concept of 'sampled portion' and calculation of incremental samples. Local inspectors use a sampling protocol for official sampling. This protocol contains information ­ among others ­ on the type of product, the target species, the total quantity of the product and the size of the sampled portion, which is in line with the requirements of points 10 of Annex 1 to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. Local inspectors have to specify if the sample was taken for detection of Salmonella and/or for other specific analyses (e.g. priority analyses). The audit team noted that since normally the feed headquarters decides on the substances to be checked for (see finding 33); the samplers are not always in position to decide whether to follow the procedure for heterogeneous or homogeneous distribution of substance(s). Conclusion on the planning and implementation of sampling

The system in place for planning of official sampling is effective and risk-based. In one of the slaughterhouses visited, Part 1 of the FCI is completed and signed by the keeper of the equine animal, Part 2 is completed and signed by the haulier and Part 3 is completed and signed by the FBO. In the other slaughterhouses visited, the FCI was always completed and signed by the FBO responsible for the holding adjacent to the 23 slaughterhouse. It was noted that the FCI never indicates the use of medicines and there was no indication that this information had been requested from the previous owner of the animal. The keeper met at one slaughterhouse explained that he relies on the oral statement and the information reported in the passports. None of the passports checked by the audit team contained a record of any medical treatment. Possible treatments at holdings of traders are not recorded. As a consequence, the reliability of the FCI cannot be properly verified. 5.4.3.2 Animal welfare

All PVP registered by the Veterinary Council are allowed to use veterinary medicines, including in cascade use, and they are the solely authorised persons to perform the identification by inserting the transponder and the verification of the markings. The CAs stated that it is PVPs' responsibility to prescribe the medical treatment and record it in the horse passport.

From the minutes of the meetings of the Equine Liaison Group of 2016 and 2017 it emerges that there are some concerns around the use of medication in the horse industry. Key areas needing particular attention were: a. Record keeping/recording of medicines administered in the passport and the non- availability of passports when animals are being treated, leading to the passport not being endorsed with medical treatments, as required; b. Accurate administration of medicines, particularly relating to the use of medicines (such as phenylbutazone) which can be mixed in with feed, leading to some of the treatments accidentally transferred to other horses for which it was not intended; c. Scarcity of approved medicines for horses, leading to the use of unauthorised/exceptional medicines, usually (but not necessarily) used via cascade rules and prescribed by PVPs.

The CA in the slaughterhouses carries out the verification of the eligibility of horses for slaughter for human consumption in a meticulous way, allowing the detection non- compliances and irregularities. The system ensures that only horses with correct identification and clearance for slaughter enter the food chain. However, the virtually complete absence of records of the medical treatments in the passports, together with the scarce verification of compliance with the requirements on prescription and correct recording of the applied treatments in the horse passports, reduces the confidence that only horses which are eligible for human consumption are presented for slaughter.

The official controls pay limited attention to the fate of the quite large amount of horses which are not eligible for slaughter for human consumption, and of the veracity of the information in passports concerning medical treatments. This diminishes the effect of the otherwise robust controls in the slaughterhouses. 29

recommendations.text: To ensure that the prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources for animal welfare reflect the objectives of the Multi-annual National Control Plan (MANCP) as required in Article 110(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: In line with the requirements of Articles 109 (1) and 110 (1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, the thesis for animal welfare is at the heart of the DAFM's strategy, the MANCP. The (2018-2022) MANCP, section 1.2, includes the National strategic objectives with two of these objectives being relevant for animal welfare: Objective 2: The enforcement of food and feed law, animal health and animal welfare rules and plant health rules. Objective 4: The co-ordination of official controls, to ensure effective and efficient implementation at national, regional and local level official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency, impartiality, quality and consistency of official controls In addition, in section 4.1, it describes the specific objectives for animal welfare: Ensure compliance with EU and national legislative requirements Improve the health status of farmed animals Ensure the welfare of animals on farm 3 There is no further description of how to achieve those objectives (by means of breaking them down to operational objectives) and how to demonstrate the extent of meeting those objectives. The authorities have not set baselines to measure the outcomes for animal welfare objectives in the MANCP. It also does not detail how the prioritisation of official controls and allocation of resources reflect those objectives contrary to the requirement of Article 110 (2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

DAFM has not translated its objectives into operational objectives and there is no indication on how the prioritisation of official controls and allocation of resources reflect those objectives. With this, DAFM misses the opportunity to demonstrate the level of compliance with AW legislation ensured, whether they are meeting their objectives and achieving demonstrable animal welfare improvements at farm level.

The FPD Programme for broilers uses slaughter plant data since 2017 and is designed as follows: Each incidence over 50% FPD in a slaughter cohort triggers a welfare notification that is received centrally. Previously, the cut-off point was 70% but it was amended reflecting improvement of the recorded performance. This notification is collated in a database to generate a league table of flocks or houses, At RVO level, they choose the flocks or houses at the top of the league- i.e. the ones with more problems. The officials open a FPD "Case" for the flock/house identified. The Case is followed with a regulatory visit and either the farm takes effective measures to address the welfare deficits identified or the officials close the house until the operator submits an action plan dealing with the outstanding welfare deficits. Following an FPD visit, the farmer is informed of the observations made and the welfare deficits identified. If the officials raise observations on three visits then 4 http://www1.clermont.inra.fr/wq/index.php?id=protocol&prod 10 they identify the flock house as non-compliant. In this way, the number of houses that are persistently associated with FPD will decrease over time. Thus, a baseline of FPD incidence has been established. The current target is to achieve the elimination of 5-10 flock houses each year from the top of the league table. The described methodology is not formalised in a procedure nor is FPD referred to in the MANCP or linked to a strategic objective.

recommendations.text: To ensure that, in accordance with the requirements of Article 5 and Article 12(1),(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, they have: procedures and/or arrangements to ensure the impartiality, quality and consistency of official controls and other official activities at all levels; procedures and/or arrangements to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls and other official activities; and control verification procedures.

citations.text: DAFM introduced a new checklist for broiler inspections that focusses on legal requirements related to footpad dermatitis (FPD). Whilst this is very comprehensive for FPD, it does not cover all the legal requirements of Council Directive 2007/43/EC e.g. mortality. This means that it cannot fully serve as the tool to ensure compliance by checking and identifying different animal welfare issues at broiler farms. In addition, there is currently no instruction/procedure in place for the performance of official controls on broiler welfare at the farms. The available material for inspectors is a training presentation dating back to 2012, which means that apart from this not being a procedure, several essential points are outdated or missing contrary to the requirements of Articles 5 and 12 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

DAFM introduced a new checklist for pig farm inspections that focusses on legal requirements related to tail docking. This too does not cover all the legal requirements of Council Directive 2008/120/EC and therefore cannot serve as a tool to ensure compliance with animal welfare requirements. 4

The competent authorities (central and regional level) supervise the performance of official controls. To date, none of the audits or supervision activities (or other means of verification e.g. analysis) have assessed the system for setting objectives and indicators (measurement system) and its performance. The supervision activities lack a control verification procedure, contrary to the requirement of Article 12 (2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. A draft procedure for the verification of effectiveness of official controls is currently under internal consultation. DAFM officials described a challenge in ensuring consistency of official controls with a meaningful example: finding many non- compliances might mean a more thorough inspection, and/or a problematic farm. On that, each inspection report must be reviewed and signed off by the supervising officer. In addition to the provision of training, veterinary inspectors from the Central Competent Authority will on occasion accompany RVO inspectors during welfare inspections in order to verify the correct implementation of inspections. There have been numerous on-site training/verification sessions for these inspections, the Pig Tails Pilot, Dairy Herds, FPD Visits and pre-registration of pig holdings inspections, to ensure consistency in application of new regulatory methods.

DAFM has not translated its objectives into operational objectives and there is no indication on how the prioritisation of official controls and allocation of resources reflect those objectives. With this, DAFM misses the opportunity to demonstrate the level of compliance with AW legislation ensured, whether they are meeting their objectives and achieving demonstrable animal welfare improvements at farm level.

In this respect, the system follows the use of an evidence-based approach by making use of the existing statistics, administrative data and the proposed monitoring framework. Reporting of welfare issues found in the broiler slaughterhouses provides an informational basis for the RVOs that receive it. However, to be effective, this aspect requires clear guidance and an appropriate follow-up mechanism so that in certain cases farms that present a certain degree of animal welfare deficiencies undergo closer monitoring and if needed inspections and further enforcement. The lack of arrangements in this respect and the non-binding nature of the reports forwarded from slaughterhouses means that DAFM does not take corrective actions based on these reports. This is not in line with the requirements for follow-up described in Annex III to Directive 2007/43/EC and reduces the impact of the official controls.

DAFM has put in place a range of tools and developed methodologies in order to gather information and report the results of the official controls internally and to the stakeholders, including the EU Commission. Reporting does not fully support the development and use of indicators, which means that DAFM misses the opportunity to integrate the available data and tools in order to reflect the overall status of animal welfare at farms and improve it.

The inadequate enforcement of certain legal requirements (pig stocking densities, routine tail docking in pigs) and the lack of arrangements to ensure that actions are taken as a follow-up to monitoring at the slaughterhouse (broiler sector) reduce the effectiveness of the official controls. 9

recommendations.text: To ensure that the prioritisation of official controls considers all risk factors and defines the regular and appropriate frequency of official controls in line with Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The competent authority has put in place a methodology to base its controls on risk. The planning process differentiates between species and it prioritises based on risks deployed by the competent authority. The central level issues lists of flocks/herds for targeted welfare inspections to DAFM's Regional Veterinary Offices (RVOs) on an annual basis. The majority are selected on a risk basis. The parameters they use to assess risk include for example: Herd/flock size; Movement/birth/mortality rates; A Cross Divisional Animal Welfare Report for that herd/flock (a system identifying a herd/flock at an animal market, slaughter plant, assembly centre, etc. as a welfare risk and reporting the flock to the relevant RVO for follow up); Local knowledge and compliance history; Presence of a specific welfare indicator e.g. tail docking in pigs, FPD in broilers. Identifying farms with a heightened risk of non-compliance and determining the reasons behind the deficiencies at farms is an evidence-based process. The available information reflects the picture at the farms and can support informed decisions on planning of official controls. However, the risk prioritisation of controls does not consider all relevant factors described in Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 for risk basis of official controls. In addition, DAFM has not defined what the regular and appropriate frequency of controls is.

The evidence and risk-based prioritisation system for official controls is systematic and focussed but it does not consider all necessary factors and has not defined the regularity and appropriate frequency of the official controls. Therefore, they might use wrong or incomplete assumptions when selecting the farms to control.

responses.response: controls DAFM will review its system for selecting herds/flocks for risk based controls in ar and relation to all species. recommendations.text: To align the current roles of staff performing/involved in official controls with the provisions of Article 18(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, and to ensure that they perform their tasks in line with the associated requirements of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. This applies, in particular, to the duties performed by local authority temporary veterinary inspectors and the associated training requireme to 35

citations.text: Moreover, delays in bringing the national rules in line with other requirements of EU Regulations result in delays or a lack of implementation of certain EU requirements by, and applicable to, the CA (see paragraphs 16, 33, 34, 67, 71, 81, 93 and 94). It should, however, be noted that the CA obligations in relation to a number of the identified issues, highlighted as being associated with more recent EU legislation, were already mandatory under previous EU law and should therefore have already been incorporated. The same applies to certain obligations of the FBOs (e.g. those of Points 2 and 6 of Chapter VI, Section I, Annex III, Point 3 (f), Section III, Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004).

FSAI and DAFM have mechanisms in place to ensure that EU provisions are subject to official controls and enforced at national level. However, delays occur in making the changes in national rules required to bring them into full compliance with EU legislation, which may affect controls over, and enforcement of, requirements applicable to FBOs and, as established during this audit, the correct and timely implementation of EU requirements in respect of CA controls.

At the time of the audit, discussions on points i. to iii. remained inconclusive and, as a result, outstanding issues related to these points had not been addressed. 5.2.2 Impartiality, freedom from conflict of interest

DAFM started formal training of TVIs in 2019. This initially involved one day class training and then 30 hours on-the-job training in a slaughter plant. The latter has been reduced to 18 hours, with the possibility of further reducing the minimum requirement, as necessary, due to the COVID-19 pandemic. · The class training covers general aspects (e.g. health and safety, conflict of interest) and specifics of TVI role in red meat slaughter (e.g. animal welfare and health, traceability, cleanliness, food chain information (FCI), checks on specified risk material, examples of abnormalities at AMI and PMI) and actions to be taken. The audit team noted that training material for PMI of red meat mentions that the head is to be inspected only if used for human consumption. This is not in line with Article 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 nor, indeed, with the same provisions set out in Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council which preceded it. · Following class training and the on-the-job training, a VI assesses the ability of applicant TVIs to do the job. TVIs that pass are placed on the panel of a slaughter plant.

Unlike DAFM, LAs do not have a system in place to ensure that their LAVIs undergo practical training for a probationary period of at least 200 hours, under the supervision of a qualified OV, before starting to work independently.

The overall operational control framework in LA does not match that of DAFM, either in terms of available resources, training of staff (while performing equivalent (OV) duties), arrangements to avoid/address possible conflict of interest, or supervision of the performance of controls. The considerable differences between the two CAs in respect of the above are detrimental to ensuring consistent official controls over, and enforcement in, the same type of establishments, including of comparable sizes. This results in diverging outcomes of DAFM and LA controls over equally applicable EU requirements, and inadequacies in the LA controls of such establishments.

A number of the above issues have been identified and recognised by the FSAI, which has made proposals aimed at addressing the challenges at LA level and the future delivery of LA controls. The absence of decisions in this respect at the time of the audit impacts on the country's ability to arrive at, and ensure, consistency between DAFM and LA official controls and enforcement of the same legal framework.

citations.text: New EU Regulations and amendments to existing EU Regulations in the agri-food chain have to be deemed as "food legislation" under national legislation, through amendments of the relevant Schedules in the FSAI Act, before they fall within the remit of the contracts with DAFM and LAVS. The latest amendment of the FSAI Act, at the time of the audit, included EU legislation up to and including 31 March 2021. EU Regulations adopted after that date were not included in the S.I. at the time of this audit. Consequently, the CAs are not legally bound to verify and enforce food business operators (FBOs)'compliance with those provisions applicable to them until such time that they are incorporated into the relevant FSAI Act Schedule.

Moreover, delays in bringing the national rules in line with other requirements of EU Regulations result in delays or a lack of implementation of certain EU requirements by, and applicable to, the CA (see paragraphs 16, 33, 34, 67, 71, 81, 93 and 94). It should, however, be noted that the CA obligations in relation to a number of the identified issues, highlighted as being associated with more recent EU legislation, were already mandatory under previous EU law and should therefore have already been incorporated. The same applies to certain obligations of the FBOs (e.g. those of Points 2 and 6 of Chapter VI, Section I, Annex III, Point 3 (f), Section III, Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004).

FSAI and DAFM have mechanisms in place to ensure that EU provisions are subject to official controls and enforced at national level. However, delays occur in making the changes in national rules required to bring them into full compliance with EU legislation, which may affect controls over, and enforcement of, requirements applicable to FBOs and, as established during this audit, the correct and timely implementation of EU requirements in respect of CA controls.

At the time of the audit, discussions on points i. to iii. remained inconclusive and, as a result, outstanding issues related to these points had not been addressed. 5.2.2 Impartiality, freedom from conflict of interest

AMI of bovine animals on the holding of provenance, for reasons other than emergency slaughter, is carried out by private veterinary practitioners, not by OVs. When it takes place, the system for emergency slaughter is used (see paragraphs 93 and 94). No arrangements are in place to give effect to the requirements of Chapter VIa of Section I, Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, and the provision of Article 31(c) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/2235 in respect of the model certificate to be used for such slaughter, is not implemented.

Nonetheless, the procedures require the private veterinarian (not an OV) to carry out the AMI at the holding of provenance. This is not in line with Article 5(2)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. DAFM has not yet assigned OVs for this task, and LA veterinarians are not legally authorised to access farms. If the AMI is favourable, the private veterinarian or slaughterhouse staff holding the required certificate of competence, performs the emergency slaughter. 18

The official certificate for emergency slaughter used nationally differs from the model set out in Chapter 5 of Annex IV \ to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/2235, as do the arrangements in place. For example, the signing veterinarian is not an OV, and is neither required to declare the date and time of slaughter, nor that the slaughter and bleeding were carried out correctly. Other official controls at slaughterhouse level

The procedures for slaughter of cattle on-farm were not aligned with the applicable EU legislation, resulting in OV duties being performed by private veterinarians and certain EU requirements not being implemented nor certified in line with these requirements.

recommendations.text: To review the arrangements in place for ante- and post-mortem inspection and to ensure: · the consistency is in line with Article 5(1)(b) of the OCR, between DAFM and local authority related requirements; · that adequate arrangements are in place for the performance of these tasks in establishments approved by the local authority; 24 · that, when benefiting from the derogations provided for in Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624, competent authorities comply with the provisions of paragraphs 1(c) and (3) of the same Article.

citations.text: The overall operational control framework in LA does not match that of DAFM, either in terms of available resources, training of staff (while performing equivalent (OV) duties), arrangements to avoid/address possible conflict of interest, or supervision of the performance of controls. The considerable differences between the two CAs in respect of the above are detrimental to ensuring consistent official controls over, and enforcement in, the same type of establishments, including of comparable sizes. This results in diverging outcomes of DAFM and LA controls over equally applicable EU requirements, and inadequacies in the LA controls of such establishments.

In DAFM plants, TAOs perform certain tasks that, according to Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624 are tasks of an OA. For example, verification of FCI, identification checks, and some welfare checks. They inform the TVI/VI of their findings. Nonetheless, contrary to the requirements of the same Article; · the OV does not regularly verify that TAOs carry out their practical tasks properly. TAOs' work is supervised by SAOs. DAFM does not consider TAOs to be OAs for the purpose of AMI; · TAOs perform the practical tasks for all bovine animals (e.g. including those from herds that have not been declared officially free of tuberculosis).

The DAFM TVIs and VIs interviewed were aware of the relevant requirements for AMI and PMI of bovine animals and of the decisions to be taken, including for findings that are more frequently seen in cull cows. In two of the LA plants, the LA TVIs were not available to be interviewed by the audit team. The reports of the DAFM visits in one of these plants noted, amongst other, inadequate arrangements to conduct AMI, due to difficult access to the limited sized lairage pens, with the FBO reading the animal tags in the trailers. The LAVI had repeatedly highlighted inadequate lairage facilities for AMI as 15 an issue, which is also mentioned in the FSAI-LA reports and corrective action requests. Nonetheless, and despite the issue not having been addressed, slaughter continued.

LA procedures describe the identification requirements and checks that are to be carried out by the TVI/VI. Animals must be accompanied by the movement permission issued by AIM (ER 106 form). Carcases are not health-marked if this form is missing. TVIs check whether ear tags match the ER 106 form, in 5% of the animals. TVIs have no access to the database, although LA staff may have. There is no LA procedure for TVIs/LAVIs to deal with identification issues.

In DAFM plants, TAOs check the FCI and record the results on the AMI record used by the TVI. In LA plants, TVIs carry out FCI checks. The report of a DAFM visit in one of the LA plants mentions that the FBO was not aware of her/his role in checking the FCI prior to presentation of the animals for AMI. This (longstanding) non-compliance had not been previously identified by the LAs.

DAFM has procedures in place to arrange for sampling for residues when AMI and/or PMI findings lead TVI to suspect breaches of legislation on chemical residues or contaminants. This did not happen in the LA examined by the audit team, as the LA TVIs are not authorised to take samples and the LAVI, authorised to take samples, may not be available to do so. AMI procedures for poultry

The TVI may contact the LAVI to carry out controls and sample detained carcases (e.g. for Bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) testing, detection of tuberculosis lesions); some exchanges in this regard were presented to the audit team. However, as regards residues sampling, this did not happen in one of the LA interviewed, and which attributed this to the LAVI not being present (TVIs are not authorised to take samples for residues). Under the circumstance, the LA did not fully apply the requirements of Article 14(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 on laboratory testing for reaching a definitive diagnosis of a suspected hazard or detecting the presence of chemical residues.

That enforcement action, initiated in 2020, was not fully effective: the report of a visit by DAFM in the same plant in 2021 still identified issues preventing PMI to be performed correctly (final carcase inspection in congested chiller without access to higher parts, livers discarded and gastro-intestinal tract removed before being presented for PMI). 17

In another LA plant, the DAFM report also noted, amongst others, "very significant concerns" linked to PMI: unsatisfactory facilities for inspection of offal - no dedicated inspection point on red offal rail, not all red offal presented for inspection, no knife steriliser for the TVI; TVI attempting to conduct inspection under conditions giving rise to health and safety concerns.

The LAVIs for these plants clarified that in the first plant the DAFM findings had been addressed, while in the second the LAVI considered that, notwithstanding the challenging conditions, all aspects of PMI were compliant. The FBO of this plant had presented plans for construction (halted due to COVID-19 restrictions) with a view to, amongst others, increase space for red and green offal handling and inspection. PMI procedures for poultry

The AMI and PMI at slaughterhouse level are organised to cover the relevant elements for bovine slaughter (including of cull cows) and poultry. Some long-term arrangements that do not allow adequate performance of AMI and PMI had been accepted by the LAs, with divergent DAFM and LA assessments of the same arrangements.

citations.text: Both DAFM VIs and LAVIs are required to keep the approval of establishments under review.
