recommendations.text: To review the arrangements in place for the official controls carried out by the local authority veterinary service and put the required measures in place to ensure the consistency and effectiveness of these controls as required by Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, in particular as regards animal welfare, hygiene and animal by-products requireme

citations.text: At central level, in brief: · The FSAI delivers its overall responsibility for the enforcement of food safety legislation on the production chain of bovine meat (after primary production), through service contracts with DAFM and LAs. It is also responsible for co-ordinating control activities between DAFM and LAs, and for ensuring consistent performance of controls; · DAFM is responsible for developing policy and legislation, as well as implementing EU rules in national law. It is also responsible for official controls in medium and large bovine and poultry slaughterhouses, delivered through its regional and local staff; · FSAI responsibilities do not cover animal health and animal welfare controls, as that legislation is not deemed "food legislation" under the FSAI Act. DAFM, as a CCA for animal health and welfare, does not have contractual arrangements with the LAs for the controls over and enforcement of the rules that fall outside FSAI's remit. See paragraph 44.

There is no regional or central structure for LAs. Some LAVS perform official controls in more than one county. In most cases, one person per county/group of counties is in 5 charge of the official controls as the CA (see also paragraph 42). Official controls in bovine and poultry slaughterhouses are implemented by 24 LAVS, under service contracts with FSAI. The Local Authority Veterinary Inspectors (LAVIs), employed to perform OV duties, are not required to be present during slaughter. They carry out audits and inspections of the FBO as well as oversight over TVIs. The TVIs carry out the AMI and PMI.

At the time of the audit, discussions on points i. to iii. remained inconclusive and, as a result, outstanding issues related to these points had not been addressed. 5.2.2 Impartiality, freedom from conflict of interest

The audit found that differences in the staffing levels of DAFM compared to LAs are maintained when plants under LA supervision grow to sizes comparable to those of plants under DAFM supervision. In two comparable facilities, DAFM availed of a permanently present VI, three TVIs, a TAO and visiting SAO and RSVI, while the LA employed two TVIs and a visiting LAVI. The last internal audit (see paragraph 37) of this LA identified a lack of sufficient manpower to carry out all necessary official controls.

The same LA audit report highlighted that controls, other than AMI, PMI and sampling, were carried out on a reactive rather than a proactive basis, and concluded that, due to the lack of a strategic approach and sufficient manpower, controls in line with the requirements were not necessarily ensured. At the time of the current audit, one LAVI continued to carry out all the veterinary controls in the LA, except AMI and PMI.

Although the CAs mentioned resource constraints linked to Brexit and the COVID-19 pandemic, the overall figures for controls in establishments in the scope of this audit suggest that the planned controls were largely implemented in the past 2 years; sometimes, additional controls were carried out. LAs reviewed by the audit team attributed the current audit's findings on the lack of consistency and in some cases of the effectiveness of controls, to resource issues. 7

The official control staff interviewed during this audit indicated an overall adequate understanding of their responsibilities, according to the procedures in place, and of the legal requirements on the topics on which they were questioned. Nonetheless, reports following FSAI and DAFM visits in LA plants indicate that certain non-compliances went undetected or that certain requirements were not adequately enforced (see paragraphs 72, 77, 87, 88, 97 to 100 and 109 to 112). 5.2.5 Supervision and Audits

The work of LAVIs is not routinely supervised. LAs' internal audits by another LA - meant to cover all areas of activity under the OCR within a five-year cycle - are peer- review exercises, given that each LA is considered a CA. There are significant differences between the reports produced by different LAs, which suggests that the approach is not standardised. The FSAI highlighted that there is ongoing work to harmonise the approach of the internal audits performed by LAVS.

The FSAI carries out audits of the official controls carried out by DAFM and LAs, as well as targeted audits on selected topics. The overview of FSAI audits of LAs' official controls indicates that, on average, LAs received one official control audit in the past 10 years, with some receiving 2 audits, and some none. In addition, some LAs participated in joint compliance reviews with FSAI, and/or received targeted audits.

FSAI's most recent audits on topics relevant for the scope of this audit were: on traceability and controls thereof (in 2016 and 2017); on LAs' controls over FBOs' implementation of Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 (in 2019, 2016 and 2015); on DAFM controls of approved poultry slaughterhouses, and on 2 LAs' controls over on- farm emergency slaughter (2013).

The FSAI, based on the outcome of its own audits, FSAI joint compliance reviews, LA inspections, as well as DG Health and Food Safety audits, raised concerns about the consistency and effectiveness of official controls at some LAVS-supervised establishments with the County and City Management Association (representing the Chief Executives of the LAs) in 2019.

It highlighted instances of: a) incorrect application of approval procedures (establishments being approved which should not be); b) non-compliances not being detected; c) regulatory responses being insufficient to secure compliance; d) official controls not in line with the SOPs developed by the LAVS with FSAI support, nor with the requirements of the service contracts or EU legislation on official controls. 9

In 2020, FSAI suggested that structural changes to the system could be key to improving the service, and to render it more robust and consistent in its enforcement activity. It also identified other actions, including changes to the service contract. In 2021, FSAI made a submission on LAVS reforms that it deems necessary, highlighting limitations in the efficiency/effectiveness of LAs oversight of slaughterhouses and cutting plants: · no LA veterinary technical supervision of the work of LAVI in most cases, affecting the LA's ability to verify correct and effective delivery of the controls (illustrated by examples of non-compliances gone undetected or not met with an adequate response, and of non-adherence to SOPs); · new VIs joining the service with little or no prior food law enforcement experience; in the absence of a technical hierarchy, there is no structured veterinary induction; · many LAs employing a single VI results in FBOs being regulated by the same individual for a long period of time; · many of the FBOs under LA supervision are small and micro-businesses with limited internal technical expertise; and · inconsistent alignment between required activity levels, and available VI resource.
At the time of this audit, no definitive policy decisions on the future delivery of official controls by LAs or the proposals made by the FSAI had yet been taken.

FSAI audits and support mechanisms do not cover animal welfare or animal health. DAFM established a Liaison Committee with the LAVS to discuss animal welfare and animal health control aspects, but its activities do not ensure supervision of the LA controls over animal health and welfare. DAFM controls in LA plants and one of the two LA internal audit reports reviewed by the audit team found ineffective welfare controls (see paragraphs 109-112). 5.2.6 Actions in case of non-compliance

Both DAFM and LAs interviewed by the audit team provided examples of different enforcement actions taken in case of non-compliances. Nonetheless, when DAFM visited slaughterhouses under LA supervision - in the context of possible transfer of control responsibilities from LA to DAFM - the outcome was significantly different (see paragraph 56). The non-compliances identified by DAFM had either not been previously identified by LAs, or their correction not effectively enforced to prevent their reoccurrence (see paragraphs 5, 72, 77, 87, 88, 97-100 and 109-112). While the LAs acted upon most of the non-compliances identified by DAFM, they did not fully agree with all DAFM findings. 10 Conclusions on competent authorities

DAFM has the overall organisation, resources, overall training of staff, as well supervision mechanisms in place to ensure that official controls in establishments under its remit are carried out consistently and in line with EU legislation, and that corrective actions are taken when needed. Nonetheless, DAFM does not supervise the animal welfare controls in establishments under LA supervision, which undermines its ability to perform effectively its task of ensuring consistency and effectiveness of animal welfare controls. In respect of ensuring absence of conflict of interest on the part of TVI, the arrangements are more robust in poultry and certain export establishments, than in other establishments under its remit.

The overall operational control framework in LA does not match that of DAFM, either in terms of available resources, training of staff (while performing equivalent (OV) duties), arrangements to avoid/address possible conflict of interest, or supervision of the performance of controls. The considerable differences between the two CAs in respect of the above are detrimental to ensuring consistent official controls over, and enforcement in, the same type of establishments, including of comparable sizes. This results in diverging outcomes of DAFM and LA controls over equally applicable EU requirements, and inadequacies in the LA controls of such establishments.

The delays in effectively using the existing FSAI coordination mechanisms and in CAs decision-making undermine the (effective) implementation of a number of horizontal EU requirements notably at LA level, such as the designation for certain official tasks and related derogation conditions, training requirements for staff involved in official controls, and safeguarding conflict of interest, which are of particular relevance for LA controls and the associated findings of this audit.

A number of the above issues have been identified and recognised by the FSAI, which has made proposals aimed at addressing the challenges at LA level and the future delivery of LA controls. The absence of decisions in this respect at the time of the audit impacts on the country's ability to arrive at, and ensure, consistency between DAFM and LA official controls and enforcement of the same legal framework.

Both DAFM VIs and LAVIs are required to keep the approval of establishments under review. Examples of addition or removal of approved activities from the list following CA controls were made available to the audit team. However, the two medium size bovine slaughterhouses under the supervision of the LAs and reviewed by the audit team received DAFM visits in the context of (possible) transfer of official controls requested by the LAs based on their increasing throughput: · The DAFM report, following the visit in one of these establishments, raised very significant concerns in relation to the plant's capacity (slaughter line inadequate for current throughput, see paragraph 98). This was also the main root cause indicated by the LA for the non-compliances subject to repeated enforcement in the other slaughterhouse; · In the second establishment, the LAVS re-issued the approval to reflect the S.I. 22/2020 provisions and included limits in the throughput justified by the chiller's capacity. Following the DAFM visit which identified serious, long-standing animal welfare breaches amongst other non-compliances, the LA suspended the (recently re-issued) approval.
DAFM visits concluded that one of these establishments did not comply with DAFM standards, and that the other one did not comply with the approval conditions under S.I. 22/2020. 12

DAFM explained its policy of requiring that non-compliances have been addressed at the time of approval, and prior to it taking over the official controls. Consequently, a transfer to DAFM may take as long as it takes for DAFM to deem an establishment to meet the approval standards: in one establishment, the transfer had not yet taken place despite repeated LA requests, since 2015. FSAI intends to address the transfer to DAFM of LA establishments exceeding the throughputs for which they were originally approved, in a Guidance Note.

There is a system in place aimed at granting approval to establishments in line with the EU requirements. Although both CAs follow the procedures in place, there are significant differences in the outcomes of DAFM and LAVS assessments of compliance with the approval conditions, in the same establishments. This highlights a lack of consistency between DAFM and LA controls but also, and taken together with the FSAI's own findings, that the LA cannot consistently ensure that the approval of establishments is adequately kept under review. In one case reviewed, this resulted in an establishment continuing to operate under LA supervision for years although deemed non-compliant by DAFM, and under whose remit it should fall.

Although the outcome of follow-up visits by the LAVI following the enforcement actions was considered satisfactory, a DAFM visit which took place some months later identified, amongst others, certain similar hygiene issues as well as inadequate handling of specified risk material. This suggests that, at least for some of the breaches, the corrective actions were not sufficiently effective, although deemed satisfactory by the LAVI.

In the other LA plant, the DAFM report identified issues which it deemed to be of very significant concern, amongst others in relation to/stemming from the daily numbers permitted by the LA for slaughter, for which the slaughter line and associated ancillary areas were not designed. The FBO had presented plans for extending the slaughter-line cutting capacity but, pending their completion, throughputs had not been affected.

The DAFM report also identified shortcomings not previously noted by the LAs, e.g. contamination of green offal (used for petfood - Category 3 ABP) with washings from the carcases splitting saw (Category 1 ABP); lack of changing facilities, and use of mobile toilets at the external perimeter of the premises for staff use, without adjacent hand- washing facilities.

The LAVIs reported to have taken the required action and that most of the findings reported by DAFM had been solved, including in relation to the procedures for dealing with ABP. Nonetheless, the gravity of some of these findings and their recurring character suggest that LA controls and enforcement in these plants had not been sufficiently effective.

DAFM started to enforce welfare during transport directly with the transporter at slaughterhouse level in 2019, but the VIs' approach was not yet uniform. One of the VIs interviewed and his RSVI were not aware of this DAFM approach and raised welfare 20 issues related to transport with the slaughterhouse operator, while the VI in another DAFM plant initiated enforcement action against the transporter. However, DAFM did not check whether the same transporter had been associated with non-compliances identified in other slaughterhouses when deciding whether a non-compliance was not repeated.

While in DAFM plants official controls staff may be present at the time of unloading and are present at the time of slaughter, this is not a requirement in most LAs. In practice, the TVIs may come to perform AMI, leave for other private tasks and return to perform delayed PMI. LAs did not report any animal welfare issues in the last 2 years. In the two LAs under review, the LAVI last notified DAFM in 2018 regarding an animal welfare incident during transport.

In one of the two LA slaughterhouses for which animal welfare controls were assessed, the LAVI had used the animal welfare checklists on an annual basis and, although certain non-compliances (e.g. no FBO checks of absence of life before dressing) were identified, the outcome of these controls was considered satisfactory. Nonetheless, when DAFM visited the same establishment, it identified animal welfare breaches which it deemed to warrant suspension of the FBOs' licence to slaughter. The LA acted upon these findings, took enforcement action and followed up the measures put in place by the FBO.

Following this incident, the LA requested DAFM to perform a dedicated animal welfare audit in the same establishment. The DAFM visit found, amongst other deficiencies, no evidence of monitoring/verification of the process of sticking/bleeding; a continued, considerable risk that head removal would commence before the animal's death (as noted in the previous DAFM visit); that the Animal Welfare Officer did not hold a certificate of competence; that the SOPs on animal intake and welfare from unloading to death did not adequately describe the process; and that the kill box and race were not fit for purpose.

Following the DAFM audit, the LA issued an improvement notice, followed by a suspension of the approval to slaughter given the FBO's inadequate progress. Nonetheless, in this case the LA's ability to identify and/or adequately assess the gravity of welfare non-compliances and to effectively enforce the relevant animal welfare requirements, was seriously called into question.

In the other slaughterhouse under LA supervision, the last report of an internal LA audit identified "significant weaknesses in the operating procedures of the slaughterhouse, particularly with regard to the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009" which had not been detected by the controls. The VI acted upon these findings. Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls

Animal welfare requirements at slaughter and during transport are enforced, but to a lesser extent in slaughterhouses under LA supervision. There is a lack of consistency between the DAFM and LA controls (and between controls in LAs) over animal welfare, and a lack of supervision by DAFM over these controls at LA level, but also in respect of FBOs' compliance with hygiene and ABP rules. The effectiveness of LA controls had not been adequately ensured in the LAs under review, as highlighted by the shortcomings identified in the organisation and operation of LA controls both during this audit and by the FSAI.

audits.title: Residues and contaminants in live animals and animal products

recommendations.text: To ensure that sampling is risk-based, targeted, takes into account background information and applicable criteria and that multiple sampling from the same producer is avoided.
recommendations.legal_basis: Point 1, 2 and 3 of Annex III to Directive 96/23/EC

citations.text: According to sampling procedures and additional information provided by the competent authorities, official sampling is in the most cases unannounced and unexpected as required by EU legislation (10). However, random sampling is (6) Annex IV to Directive 96/23/EC and Commission Decision 97/747/EC. (7) http://www.hpra.ie/homepage/veterinary/veterinary-medicines-information (8) Reference to their use, under exceptional circumstances and in line with Commission implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/470 of 21 March 2018 on detailed rules on the maximum residue limit to be considered for control purposes for foodstuffs derived from animals which have been treated in the EU under Article 11 of Directive 2001/82/EC. (9) Article 12 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2021/808. (10) Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Point 1 of Annex III to Directive 96/23/EC. 4 performed in a certain number of cases, due to other existing practical arrangements. In these cases, the sampling officers did not plan dedicated residue sampling events, but took advantage of other control activities planned for the same establishment (unrelated to residue monitoring and undertaken pursuant to a separate risk assessment) to take residues samples during these visits. (11)

Contrary to the requirements laid down in EU legislation (12), the auditors noted that, in many cases on aquaculture farms (13) and sometimes in slaughterhouses (horses, pigs), multiple sampling, i.e. from the same producer and animal category and for the same substances to be tested for, was performed on the same day.

For several samples taken at slaughterhouses, one sampling officer did not follow the existing procedures and guidelines regarding the selection of animals for sampling. E.g., samples for hormone testing were taken from male animals while only females should have been sampled according to the plan. The non-respect of the clear guidelines available to the sampling officer had not been identified by supervision or other verification procedures.

For bovine sampling at slaughterhouse level, targeted sampling was not always implemented. The sampling inspector interviewed had no access to information on the outcome of official controls (e.g. previous non-compliant results) or background information about the producer and the farming system. The outcome of the ante mortem inspection (e.g. sex and age of the animal, secondary sexual characteristics, behavioural changes, signs of disease or chronic disorders, different health status of specific animals within a group) was also not considered in the choice of the animal to target for sampling and not in line with the applicable legal requirements (14). Nevertheless, suspect samples were taken occasionally after all findings of veterinary ante mortem checks had been carefully considered when deciding whether stock could proceed for slaughter and whether or not laboratory testing was required to ensure the safety of the food being produced.

With regard to aquaculture sea farming, fish at smolt stage are sampled at farm level. The sampling of adult fish has been implemented only for farms harvesting during the year and selected for sampling of animals ready to be placed on the market for consumption. These animals were sampled at processing level only. Therefore, the requirement to sample fish for Group A substances at all stages of production (15) was not met.

The residue monitoring plan is generally implemented in accordance with legal requirements and planned arrangements. However, targeted sampling was not consistently ensured and the sampling strategies applied for several commodities were not adequate. In addition, the evident lack of supervision or other verification procedures, in relation to sampling officers not following the detailed instructions, contributes to the persistence of sampling errors and weakens the effectiveness of the residue monitoring. 5.1.4. Other residue monitoring programmes Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure the consistency and effectiveness of follow-up investigations of non-compliant residue results.
recommendations.legal_basis: Articles 137 and 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, Articles 4, 5 and 6 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2090.

citations.text: For one of the steroid samples the sex of the animal was not indicated in the sampling report. In another case the wrong animal sex was sampled, which was not in line with existing sampling instructions. As the sample was not discarded and still analysed by the laboratory, it led to a result for which no interpretation (as to whether illegal treatment had occurred or not) was possible.

The first follow-up step performed in relation to non-compliant results was in all cases a desk-based evaluation, called `herd profile', initiated in most of these cases within days following receipt of the non-compliant result. Furthermore, in seven of the ten files, on-farm visits were planned. For two of these the competent authority could not present any evidence that the visits had taken place (22).

Following the detection of ivermectin in bulk milk (this substance is not authorised for use in milk-producing animals in the EU), and despite the partial absence of records noted during the on-farm control and a parallel detection, below the Maximum Residue Limit (MRL), of another antiparasitic agent (closantel), the competent authority could not present during the audit any evidence that additional investigations (23) were performed. The creamery was informed by email of the (22) In their response to the draft report, the competent authority clarified that the planned visits were cancelled after having discussed these cases with the EURLs, and amendment of the initial evaluation, which took into consideration the possibility of the existence of endogenously formed hormones and the difficulties to distinguish between endogenously formed and administered hormones. (23) In their response to the draft report, the competent authority noted that additional investigations were performed and included a visit to the herd owners' veterinary practice and visits to local anthelmintic supplier outlets. 8 non-compliant result and advised that it was free to carry out further sampling of milk from this producer in the context of its own-control programme.

The legal framework for investigating non-compliant residue results is in line with the EU requirements. In most of the cases, the competent authority undertook investigations promptly when non-compliant residue results were received, and sanctions were imposed. However, in some cases follow-up actions were incomplete or non-exhaustive, and in other cases not well documented, militating against the identification of the cause of the non-compliance and thus preventing recurrence. (24) In their response to the draft report, the competent authority stated that it had requested that samples be taken next time that the herd owner presented animals for slaughter. (25) In their response to the draft report, the competent authorities stated that farm investigations were carried out. 9

recommendations.text: To ensure that all laboratories carrying out laboratory analyses of residue monitoring samples are designated as official laboratories.

citations.text: The audit team noted that the designation of the official laboratories in line with EU legislation (26) was, at the time of the audit, still ongoing and not finalised for any of the laboratories involved in the residue monitoring plan. The FSAI demonstrated a template Letter of Designation, which had been drafted in line with the requirements laid down in EU legislation (27). For the laboratories located in other EU Member States, efforts were made to ensure, in particular, that such laboratories are designated as official laboratories by the competent authority of the laboratory's home country in line with these requirements.

The fact that all laboratories are accredited, that the analytical methods used are included in their respective scopes of accreditation, that adequate internal quality controls are in place and that the laboratories have satisfactorily performed in proficiency tests, provide assurances to the competent authority on the reliability of results generated. Notwithstanding these positive aspects, the absence of formal designation of some of the laboratories and certain technical deficiencies in method validation, in particular in establishing decision limits, undermine the effectiveness of the overall residue control system.

recommendations.text: To ensure that, when methods are extended to new matrices/species, necessary supplementary studies are carried out and adequately documented.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 3 of, and Chapter 4 of Annex I to, Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808.

citations.text: With regard to the validation of the confirmatory methods checked by the audit team, all relevant species/tissues were included in the validation. However, in one case (confirmatory method for tetracyclines and 4-epimers in muscle), studies on recovery, repeatability and reproducibility, based on the validation file submitted, were carried out only in bovine muscle while the method is used also for testing muscle of ovine, porcine, avian, cervine and equine animals. In two other cases (confirmatory methods for (i) anthelmintics, and (ii) dyes ­ both in aquaculture), the validation was carried out on wild salmon matrix and, partially, for prawns while the method is applied to other finfish, e.g. trout. The laboratory representative explained that the practical experience had demonstrated that the differences in the matrices were negligible, however, no documentary evidence of such comparison was presented by the laboratory. Such an approach is not fully in line with the requirements of EU legislation (31).

The fact that all laboratories are accredited, that the analytical methods used are included in their respective scopes of accreditation, that adequate internal quality controls are in place and that the laboratories have satisfactorily performed in proficiency tests, provide assurances to the competent authority on the reliability of results generated. Notwithstanding these positive aspects, the absence of formal designation of some of the laboratories and certain technical deficiencies in method validation, in particular in establishing decision limits, undermine the effectiveness of the overall residue control system.

responses.response: In the context of Ireland's comments in relation to this finding, an e- information system has been designated by the CA, to facilitate notification to DAFM of consignments subject to requirements of Article 37 (4a) of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2124 and which provides for verification of compliance by operators with all provisions of Article 37 regarding re-entry to the EU following transit through a Third Country. citations.text: The audit team evaluated 17 CHED-Ps for consignments of goods of animal origin entering the EU and noted that all consignments were subject to documentary checks, and identity checks, in line with Article 49(1) of the OCR. This does not allow to confirm whether the controls are effective in achieving their intended purpose, whether verification checks detect any issues and whether the authorities take timely corrective actions to improve the effectiveness of official controls when needed.

The competent authorities use the wide range of effective and proportionate enforcement actions available when non-compliances are detected. They promptly suspend transporters, drivers and/or vehicle certificates if necessary to bring operators to take the desired corrective actions and comply with EU animal welfare requirements. However, as the Irish authorities do not interpret Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 as creating a legal obligation to feed unweaned calves on a ferry journey from Ireland to neighbouring Member States, they do not enforce feeding the animals on the ferry. 6 FINDINGS ON FRAMEWORK FOR OFFICIAL CONTROLS AND OTHER OFFICIAL ACTIVITIES The key strengths of the official control system are comprehensive documented procedures prioritising the transport of unweaned calves and introducing stricter and additional measures and controls, effective and proportionate enforcement actions, and regular communication and cooperation with the French competent authorities. The key weaknesses are a few gaps in documented procedures particularly on feeding unweaned calves during the sea part of the journey on roll-on roll-off vessels, and the lack of records on the outcome of verification of official controls.

citations.text: Sampling of imported fresh meat covered sampling at two seaport BCPs only. Contrary to the requirements of point 3.3 (a) of part A of the Annex to the EU Decision, the two airport BCPs designated for imports of fresh meat were not included in the sampling plan. In 2021 and 2022, a small number of consignments were received at Dublin Airport. These consisted of a small number of boxes and were considered by the DAFM as possibly high value food samples. It could not be established if any of the consignments were eligible for sampling.

A very limited number of samples were taken at the seaport BCPs in 2021 and 2022. This number was well below the minimum numbers set out in the EU Decision. According to the DAFM, among other things, the following reasons contributed to that low number: a) The relevant SOPs advised that i) only packed meat could be sampled, and ii) samples were to be taken only if they could be sent to the laboratory in their original sealed packaging. This excluded some commercial presentations, such as bulk consignment with loose cuts of meat or whole carcasses (7,8). This exclusion is not (6) In their response to the draft report, the competent authorities noted that the SOP for sampling of meat at retail has been amended to include sampling of loose meat. (7) The DAFM stated that aside from being considered unpacked meat, whole carcasses were also excluded from sampling because of health and safety concerns (for frozen meat) and the risk of damaging a high value product. (8) In their response to the draft report, the competent authorities noted that the SOP for sampling of meat at BCPs has been amended to include sampling of loose packed meat. 10 in line with the relevant provisions of point 3.3 (a) of part A of the Annex to the EU Decision and EFSA technical specifications. b) The complexities derived from Brexit. These included i) the Trade Control and Expert System - New Technology (TRACES-NT) did not capture consignments from the United Kingdom before it became a third country ii). Brexit caused a very substantial increase in the consignments of products of animal origin intended for human consumption presented to Dublin Port BCP, iii) specific type of mixed consignments which made identifying the eligible consignment and product at documentary checks and on presentation for inspection very resource intensive, and iv) peak BCP workloads and resource requirements, inspecting United Kingdom origin consignments, as multiple ferries arrive within short time periods. Conclusions on sampling

The competent authority has documented procedures in place to support the implementation of most of the provisions laid down in the EU Decision, and this implementation is largely satisfactory. However, the exclusion of unpacked meat at BCPs and the exclusion of small BCPs from the sampling plan negatively affects the representativeness of the data.

recommendations.text: FSAI should ensure that the competences on public health for aquaculture are unequivocally assigned to an official agency in line with Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, and documented procedures for the performance of official controls are developed accordingly.

citations.text: The audit team identified a designation gap concerning the competencies on public health controls for aquaculture farms that are not formally assigned in the service contracts from FSAI to MI or DAFM. According to MI, they are the CA for the implementation of aquatic animal health controls and have no role in public health. This designation gap is not in line with Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The MI documented procedures for aquaculture farms are designed for fish health controls and not for public health. Nonetheless, the current checks for biosecurity in fish health broadly cover the public health requirements for primary production (e.g. hygiene and disinfection, waste removal, staff training, excessive mortality etc.). However, in the absence of dedicated public health procedures (e.g. checklists), from a cursory review of documentation the audit team could not readily verify to what extent public health issues are taken into account during controls nor of the obligation to do so.

The CAs are designated for the performance of official controls throughout the production chain, except for public health controls at aquaculture farms. Consequently, in the controls in the aquaculture area there is a reliance on controls that are designed and carried out primarily for animal health purposes.

recommendations.text: DAFM should ensure that the inspectors carrying out official controls in cold stores receive adequate training regarding the relevant requirements for fishery products and the operations performed, in line with Article 5 (4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: According to FSAI, extensive training was provided in 2016 to DAFM officials responsible for cold stores, to address the 2014 audit report findings, but there is no training plan. An induction training for newcomers is in place. It consists of a 200 hours "mentoring programme" provided by a senior official and general training, which includes a ten-hour module for cold stores. However, the audit team noted that the training records provided do not include any reference to fishery products requirements. The DAFM officials interviewed (newcomers and seniors officials) were not knowledgeable on basic requirements applicable to fishery products. This situation was acknowledged by DAFM representatives. This is not in line with Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The gaps in the training and knowledge on fishery products of DAFM officials responsible for performing controls in stand-alone cold stores, combined with the lack of requirements/instructions for fishery products, has led to the absence of official controls on key requirements for fishery products in such establishments.

According to DAFM inspectors, they never check and or ask the operator to check the core temperature of the fishery products. One cold store operator had a "goods intake procedure" setting a maximum temperature of -15°C for frozen products, but without setting corrective actions for products not reaching this temperature. This is not in line with Section VIII, Chapter VII (2), and Chapter VIII (1)(b) of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. DAFM inspectors were not aware of these requirements. According to the cold store representative, frozen fish received at any temperature above -15°C is accepted and undergoes blast freezing.

recommendations.text: DAFM should review the documented procedures to include relevant requirements for fishery products in line with Article 12 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. DAFM should also perform relevant controls in fishery products according to Article 70 and Chapter I of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. In both cases, operations performed in cold stores such as freezing, thawing and chilled and frozen storage should be included in the documented procedures and official controls.

citations.text: DAFM checklists or inspectors' instructions for cold stores do not include references to the basic requirements for fishery products for the activities performed in such establishments. DAFM acknowledged this situation. This is not in line with Article 12 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The gaps in the training and knowledge on fishery products of DAFM officials responsible for performing controls in stand-alone cold stores, combined with the lack of requirements/instructions for fishery products, has led to the absence of official controls on key requirements for fishery products in such establishments.

According to DAFM inspectors, they never check and or ask the operator to check the core temperature of the fishery products. One cold store operator had a "goods intake procedure" setting a maximum temperature of -15°C for frozen products, but without setting corrective actions for products not reaching this temperature. This is not in line with Section VIII, Chapter VII (2), and Chapter VIII (1)(b) of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. DAFM inspectors were not aware of these requirements. According to the cold store representative, frozen fish received at any temperature above -15°C is accepted and undergoes blast freezing.

The audit team noted several boxes of smoked salmon labelled "refrigerated 0-4°C". The expiry date on the label was exceeded by five months at the time of the visit. According to DAFM and SFPA the product was received chilled, and blast frozen at the owner's request.

The salmon's producer sets a use-by period of 28 days for refrigerated smoked salmon. If the salmon is later frozen, they would relabel the product, modifying the batch code to add 9 "defrosted" and indicating a new use-by period of 21 days after thawing. In the meanwhile, the product is kept in the cold store with the old label, even if the date has expired, with no indication of the maximum period that it can be kept frozen.

The actions taken by DAFM and SFPA officials to investigate this finding, at the audit team's request, were satisfactory. According to the information provided by the CA, the operator did not avail of a validated shelf study to demonstrate compliance with the relevant microbiological criteria set out in Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 (supporting the 21 days period for the use-by date of the thawed smoked salmon, after being frozen and defrosted). 5.3.1.6 Freezer and factory vessels

The DAFM official controls in stand-alone cold stores do not cover the relevant requirements for fishery products. 5.3.2 Official controls of fishery products Legal requirements Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Articles 70, 71 and Chapter I of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Findings

According to the DAFM officials, they regularly take samples at the request of the DAFM laboratories. However, in the cold store visited, they have never carried out controls on fishery products, taken samples for analysis or checked the specific labelling requirements for fishery products. This is not in line with Article 70 and Chapter I of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Conclusion on official controls of fishery products

While official controls of fishery products include all the relevant elements, these controls are generally applied throughout the supply chain, with the exception of stand-alone cold stores under DAFM responsibility.

recommendations.text: SFPA should ensure that inspections are performed without prior notice, except if duly justified, as indicated in Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: DAFM, SFPA and MI have the required powers to access on-land premises. Regarding vessels, SFPA shall be informed of any vessel calling to a port with a four-hour prior notice and can perform ad-hoc visits regarding their fisheries competencies. SFPA's inspectors make case-by-case arrangements with the vessel's owner to perform an announced public health inspection. The SFPA has the power to inspect vessels when berthed.

SFPA performs inspections, generally with prior notice, which should cover all the relevant requirements during the year. In the two SFPA regions visited, 84% of inspections in one and 80% in the other, in 2022, were performed with prior notice. Up to 64% of the operators only received inspections with prior notice. The audit team identified 4 operators in different SFPA regions that underwent prior notice inspections for a period of 3 years 7 (covering up to 9 inspections) without having been "duly justified", as required by Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

According to officials, the main reason for prior notice inspections is to guarantee that the premises are in operation and those responsible are available, especially in remote areas. However, the establishments visited (mainly subject to prior notice) were not in remote locations, had predictable working shifts and the responsible staff (e.g. the quality manager) was present on a daily basis during operation. 5.3.1.2 Primary production fishing vessels

According to officials, the inspections take place with prior notice after consultation with the owner, usually when the vessel is not in operation. Inspections are generally avoided during landing to reduce the extra burden on operators and, in some regions, are clustered during low season. The audit team noted unannounced inspections at the time of berthing, despite the fact that operators did not consistently provide the four-hours prior notice of arrival.

The majority of SFPA inspections are carried out with prior notice, despite the fact that this is contrary to their own instructions and that unannounced visits could be readily performed on land-based establishments. This can negatively impact the effectiveness of official controls.

recommendations.text: SFPA should approve an establishment for the activities concerned only if the food business operator has demonstrated that it complies with the relevant requirements of food law and this should also be kept under review during official controls, in line with Article 148(3) and (5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The SFPA provided examples of approvals, in which conditional approvals were granted providing the premises met, at minimum, the structural and equipment conditions. The maximum period of 3 plus 3 months (6 plus 6 months for vessels) was not exceeded.

The audit team noted from approval reports of freezer vessels (glazing prawns) that the relevant requirements concerning potable water were not consistently assessed during approval. The inspectors requested clarification from SFPA's headquarters in relation to the assessment of potable water, but at the time of the audit, a final decision was not available.

The two vessels visited produced glazed frozen prawns and applied additives by immersion into a tank with additives. In both vessels, the approval procedures, as implemented, covered the application of additives. However, the report of the approval inspection did not document the assessment of the FBO's validation process for additive application; the inspectors acknowledged that they do not assess this and relevant equipment during approval. (see paragraph 46).

SFPA applies satisfactorily their documented approval procedures. Nonetheless, and contrary to Article 148 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, there are gaps in the application of these procedures for freezer vessels, notably related to the assessment of certain operators' validation procedures (use of additives). 6

In two of four establishments visited under SFPA control, some activities included in the approval certificate had been discontinued up to 9 years ago and were not covered by the operators' HACCP. In another case, a new activity, not fully covered by the HACCP plan, had been included in the approval certificate. This is not in line with Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004.
In the two freezer vessels visited, the dipping procedure documented in the HACCP plan was not the one applied in practice by the operative responsible.

Concerning the dipping procedure for additives, the audit team identified the following shortcomings, which were not detected by the inspectors during the visit, in at least one of the vessels: · The timer used to control the immersion bath did not work properly; · The indicated time for prawn immersion is the minimum to be used but a maximum time is not specified; · There was not a clear indication of the level to which the tank should be filled according to the dipping procedure. Therefore, the actual concentration of additive used for dipping is unclear; · Evidence of calibration of the scales was not in place; · The operator's explanation of the quantity of additive used and how it was weighed was inconsistent and was not according to the procedure; · The dipping procedure does not consider the maximum quantity of prawns that can be dipped in one bath, before discharging it; · The dipping procedure was established for a water temperature different to the standard range of temperature of the seawater in the fishing grounds. 10 The elements described above, can be a source of variability in the final concentration of additives. They are not sufficiently addressed during the assessment of the validation process carried out by the operator. In these circumstances, they may significantly influence the outcome of the dipping step and in some circumstances may lead to sulphites levels in excess of the EU limits, as detected in six RASFF alerts. This source of variability is mitigated by monitoring programmes, undertaken (in the cases seen, by the associated co-operatives) with satisfactory results.

The two freezer vessels visited were of a generally sound infrastructure. In the first vessel SFPA officials conducted an announced inspection and shortcomings of limited relevance were detected. In the second vessel, an unannounced inspection was carried out. In this case, the inspector identified a number of relevant shortcomings (i.e. the fish hold had a strong fish odour and was dirty and mouldy, with exposed wooden pallets, the concrete floor was poorly maintained, the ice machine and the pipes were rusty, and stored ice was not clean, the blast freezer presented a layer of 20 centimetres of ice on the floor containing prawns. The inspector thoroughly followed the checklist and guidance, identifying the shortcomings. However, a similar range of shortcomings had been identified in a previous inspection to this vessel (unannounced) but the audit team did not find evidence of shortcomings correction. Conclusions on official controls of production and placing on the market
In operators under SFPA control, the approval conditions, in particular concerning HACCP, are not consistently kept under review with the operation of the premises.

In some cases, the controls carried out by the inspectors on the freezing vessels do not verify that the operators follow their own procedures concerning the use of additives and that these procedures have being properly validated. As a consequence, and despite the monitoring programmes in place, there is a risk that the EU limits for additives may be exceeded.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the results of monitoring activities carried out for the purpose of Article 8 of Directive 2000/60/EC are taken into account when establishing the frequency of risk-based official controls on the marketing and use of PPPs, as required by Article 24(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The audit team noted that, among various risk criteria used by DAFM to plan their controls, the results of the water monitoring carried out for the purpose of Article 8 of Directive 2000/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council are not taken into account. This is not in line with Article 24(2)(a) of the OCR. In a position paper2 from 2019, regarding pesticides in drinking water developed by Ireland's Health Service Executive and Environmental Protection Agency, a reference is made to a total of 19 individual pesticides that account for all pesticide exceedances in drinking water reported in Ireland by the end of 2018. While at the time of development of that position paper the levels of pesticides found in Irish drinking water had not presented an 2 https://www.epa.ie/publications/compliance--enforcement/drinking-water/advice-- guidance/EPA_HSE_JPP_Pesticides_DrinkingWater---FINAL.pdf 8 appreciable risk to human health, it is stated in the position paper that any exceedance of EU parametric limits is undesirable and must be managed proactively.

The CA considers most of the relevant risks when developing the plan of controls on the marketing and use of PPPs, but the results of monitoring activities carried out for the purpose of Article 8 of Directive 2000/60/EC, as required by Article 24(2)(a) of the OCR are not taken into account, this oversight potentially compromises the protection of water bodies.

audits.title: evaluate the implementation of official controls on animal by-products (ABP) and derived products (DP)

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls in meat-producing establishments supplying material for the production of petfood, ABP processing plants and petfood manufacturing plants are effective in verifying operator compliance with applicable legal requirements.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 in conjunction with Article 4(3) and 4(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and Article 32(1), (2) and (3) of Commission Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

citations.text: The audit team examined documents accompanying consignments of ABP destined for the manufacture of petfood. On the evidence provided, the team inferred that the official controls in some of the meat-producing establishments supplying raw material to the petfood industry were ineffective given the observed non-compliances with the requirements for commercial documents and health certificates, identification and categorisation of ABP, and the collection and transport of ABP. Examples included: a. Contrary to the requirements set out in Article 21(2) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and Article 17 and Chapter III of Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, consignments were either shipped without the commercial documents/health certificates that should accompany the consignments during transport, or with incomplete (incorrectly filled-in) documents. Missing data in these documents included the approval numbers of the dispatching and/or the receiving establishment/plant, the category of ABP, information on the species of origin of the ABP and the intended use of the ABP. b. Contrary to the requirements of Article 21(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and Article 17 and Chapter II of Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, the consignments of ABP dispatched to petfood plants were not appropriately identified and notably, the obligatory warning sentence for the category of ABP describing its permitted use was missing on the containers holding the ABP. c. Rules for classification of ABP were not followed, resulting in incorrectly categorised ABP being dispatched to ABP processing plants supplying derived products to the petfood industry (see finding 44.a). 5.2.3.2 Official controls in ABP plants and petfood manufacturers

In the petfood plants, the audit team examined the operators' compliance with the requirements regarding commercial documents and health certificates, identification, the collection and transport of ABP and traceability and compared what they saw with what 9 was recorded in the inspection reports. The reports omitted the following non- compliances: a. For the manufacture of petfood, operators accepted ABP arriving either without or with incomplete commercial documents/health certificates (see finding 36.a). In particular, the documents accompanying consignments of ABP destined for the production of raw petfood did not contain information demonstrating that the ABP consisted of exclusively Category 3 material (sub-category defined in Art.10(a), (b)(i) and/or (ii) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009). b. Operators also used ABP that arrived in packaging or in containers which were not properly identified (i.e., concerning the category of ABP and the warning sentence which were missing) (see finding 36.b).

The audit team also noted that as regards the overall hygiene, cleanliness and maintenance of the plant equipment, the reports of the official controls indicated that these aspects were compliant, in marked contrast to what the audit team encountered in the establishments. It found (i) dirty containers used for collection of ABP resulting from the plant operations, (ii) dirty crates and racks used for the handling of ABP destined for thermal treatment and (iii) dirty chambers used for thermal treatment.

With regard to the operators' written procedures based on HACCP principles, the reports of the official controls did not indicate any particular issues, whereas the audit team noted that: a. Some petfood operators had in place HACCP-based procedures that were generic and not reflective of the practices taking place in the plant. For example, whilst the transport temperature for arriving ABP was considered as a critical control point (CCP), it was not monitored by the operator and the storage temperature limit which would trigger an alarm was at a much higher temperature than the limit established as a CCP. b. In all of the petfood plants visited, the HACCP-based procedures were deficient with respect to the categorisation of the ABP present in these plants. Whilst the plants generated some Category 2 material, operators collected, stored and dispatched all ABP as Category 3 material, contrary to requirements laid down in Articles 7 and 9(g) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. With one exception, the operators dispatched to ABP processing plants approved for Category 3 material (and producing processed animal protein, also destined for the manufacture of petfood), ABP which they considered to be Category 3 material, even though this consisted of a mixture of Category 2 and Category 3 materials or partly decomposed Category 3 material.

With regard to the official assessments of the operators' own-checks, in some of the petfood plants, the inspection reports did not record non-compliances identified by the audit team: a. Sampling for Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae did not follow the appropriate sampling protocol ­ the operator collected one instead of five samples. 10 b. Notwithstanding the above, the operators also incorrectly interpreted the examination results when determining the compliance of the sampled batch of petfood, contrary to the requirements laid down in point 5 (dogchews) and point 6 (raw petfood) of Chapter II of Annex XIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. For instance, the operators did not consider a result with three or more samples with a bacterial count (Enterobacteriaceae) between 10 and 300 colony forming units (cfu) in 1 gramme (dogchews) or between 500 and 5,000 cfu in 1 gramme (raw petfood) as non-compliant. Only results with bacterial counts higher than 300 or 5,000 cfu respectively were considered non-compliant. c. There was a mismatch between the examination results on microbiological standards and the information recorded for the produced batches of petfood. While the operator had results of all sampled production batches, some results could not be linked to any of the production batches, because these were not recorded in the production records.

The one ABP plant visited which was processing Category 3 material and supplying derived products (processed animal proteins of mixed species) to the petfood industry was subject to bi-annual controls (see finding 30) and daily controls were performed by the DAFM official who is present in this particular plant on a daily basis (see finding 24). The reports of these controls indicated that the plant was compliant. However, the audit team identified numerous non-compliances related to the categorisation of ABP. The overall cleanliness and hygiene in the plant was poor as was the maintenance of the processing equipment.

With respect to the categorisation of ABP, the audit team noted that Category 2 material was being used for production of mixed processed animal proteins: a. ABP from slaughterhouses arriving as Category 3, contained Category 2 material such as (i) digestive tracts with their contents, (ii) animals' heads with attached plastic eartags, (iii) animal tissues mixed with plastic and paper and (iv) by- products in a state of decomposition. b. Category 2 material originating in the processing plant was recycled into the Category 3 processing line. This Category 2 material consisted of (i) the sludge collected from water traps, (ii) ABP from another line processing material of poultry origin, and rejected due to the presence of foreign bodies, and (iii) pieces of ABP recovered from the floor and derived products (processed animal proteins) which had spilled out and was then collected from the floor.

The issues on incorrect categorisation of ABP identified in the finding above were also seen in the 2018 audit report (DG SANTE 2018-6334) and on which a recommendation (#4) was made. The actions taken by DAFM have not been effective given the recurrence of the issue.

Whilst official controls are performed on the ABP operators supplying the petfood industry and those manufacturing petfood, they are ineffective, as evidenced by the numerous non-compliances identified by the audit team in establishments deemed to be compliant by the competent authority. The fact that these issues had not been identified in the context of the regular supervisory activities or in the DAFM internal audit of the sector, additionally raises concerns about the operation of the official control system in this sector. Furthermore, some of the non-compliances were identified in the previous Commission audit, indicating that the measures taken by the competent authority to address them were ineffective. Collectively, these findings undermine official 12 assurances that operators involved in petfood production in Ireland comply with EU requirements.

responses.response: The audit acknowledged that all elements needed for an effective official control system are in place, but it was not always effective at plant level. The Department has noted the specifically referenced findings and conclusion on which this recommendation is based. With that in mind the Department has initiated actions to ensure that these matters are successfully addressed and that this is sustained going forward. ons taken to ensure effectiveness of official controls 1. citations.text: Independent cold stores handling dairy products requiring temperature-controlled condi- tions are only registered and not approved by the CA, as required by Article 4 of Regu- lation (EC) No 853/2004. The DAFM representatives stated that currently 15 cold stores fall under such conditions and are subjected to risk-based official controls.

citations.text: Cattle were correctly identified, whilst in the goat farm more than 50% of the adult ani- mals and almost the totality of the younger ones were not tagged or identified by an al- ternative method. Moreover, no actions had been taken by the private veterinarian con- tracted by the farmer, or by the private veterinarian in charge of animal health testing, to remedy the situation. This is not in line with the requirements in Article 14 of Commis- sion Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/520. The DG SANTE audit team requested further information on this regard, which was provided in the action plan of the CA.
The lack of proper identification of goat animals jeopardises both the reliability of rec- ords of medical treatments and of the animal health tests. 10

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls in ABP processing plants are effective in assessing operators' validation of their processing methods.
recommendations.legal_basis: Articles 28 and 29 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, Sections 1 and 2 in Chapter I of Annex XVI and Chapter III point G in Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

citations.text: With respect to the assessment of critical controls points, as part of the validation procedure, official controls overlooked their absence and/or their incorrect designation, contrary to requirements of Article 29 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, Chapter III point G in Annex IV and point 1 of Section 2 of Chapter I of Annex XVI to Commission Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

With respect to validation on processing parameters (for method 7 in continuous system) and validation checks, official controls overlooked that operators lacked supporting evidence to demonstrate the capacity of the processing method to reduce identified hazards to a level which does not pose any significant risks to public and animal health. This is not in line with requirements for validations laid down in Section 2 in Chapter I of Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

Regarding ABP processing plants, while official controls satisfactorily verify compliance with hygiene and infrastructural requirements, the audit team found that such controls overlooked incomplete or incorrect validation of processing methods by the operators. This limits the capacity of official controls to verify whether the processing methods can reduce relevant hazards to a level which does not pose any significant risks to public and animal health.
